Introduction

STRENGTH FOR THE JOURNEY

Every generation must decide whether they will take God at His Word. For Israel, that decision came on the edge of the Jordan River. A new leader stood before them. A land of promise stretched out ahead of them. And the God who had delivered them from Egypt now called them to move forward in faith.

That leader’s name was Joshua. His story is one of battles and blessings, failures and victories, warnings and promises. But more than that, it is the story of God’s faithfulness. Again and again, we read: “Not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you; all are come to pass unto you” (Joshua 23:14). Joshua’s life is not just ancient history—it is a living picture of the Christian life. Just as Israel had to cross the Jordan, face their enemies, and trust God’s Word, so every believer is called to step out of fear and into faith, to fight spiritual battles, and to walk in obedience. The same God who gave victory at Jericho and strength in the wilderness is the God who fights for us today. This book is not about Joshua’s greatness, but about God’s greatness displayed through an obedient servant. Joshua’s courage came not from his own strength but from God’s presence: “Be strong and of a good courage… for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Joshua 1:9). That promise still holds true for every follower of Christ.

As you read these chapters, you will find encouragement for weary days, warnings against compromise, and reminders that victory always belongs to the Lord. Joshua points us to Jesus, the Captain of our Salvation, who leads us into eternal rest and everlasting hope. The journey of Joshua is the journey of faith. And the invitation is clear: step forward, trust God, and claim the promises He has given. The same God who was faithful then is faithful still.
Chapter 1 — The First Victory

ONE IN A MILLION

Before Joshua was a leader in Canaan, he was a servant in the wilderness. He was born into Egyptian slavery, endured Pharaoh’s harsh rule, and witnessed the mighty hand of God bring plagues, part seas, and preserve a nation. He saw water gush from a rock and manna fall from heaven. He watched the Red Sea swallow the Egyptian army—and then he watched nearly all of his generation fall in the wilderness. Among two million Israelites, only two men who left Egypt would live to step foot in the Promised Land: Caleb and Joshua. Joshua was literally one in a million.

You, too, are special. You were miraculously created by Almighty God. He has a special plan and purpose for your life. He loves you. To be loved by God is life’s highest calling and greatest achievement! You are called into a love relationship with God. He knows you and wishes to reveal Himself to you and fellowship with you. Satan wants to tell you a different story. He wants to feed you the lie that you are insignificant, unloved, and useless. He whispers the false truth that God has betrayed you, abandoned you, and has left you to figure life out on your own. Satan offers false hope in substance abuse, illicit relationships, and countless other distractions to numb your doubts, questions, and pain. However, the truth is that none of this will help. Only Jesus can satisfy your soul.

Before reading any further, I challenge you to turn your heart toward God. Settle in your heart that, regardless of your current situation, God has forever proved His love for you by sending His Son, Jesus Christ, to die on the cross. (John 3:16, Romans 8:32) Accept that no matter your age, race, gender, social status, Spiritual maturity, or past, God loves you, He accepts you, and in Him, you are secure and significant! Without settling these truths in your mind, heart, and soul, the remainder of this book will be only empty words, unhelpful quotes, and unheeded Scriptures. But with the love of God in your heart, I pray this book will strengthen your faith, encourage your spirit, and renew your resolve to follow God. He will guide you into great victory, and you, like Joshua, will be one in a million!

❝ Joshua was literally one in a million ❞

FROM COMPLAINT TO COMBAT

The first time Joshua appears in Scripture, it’s not as a general, a prophet, or a miracle worker—it’s as a young man given a nearly impossible assignment: fight Amalek. (Deuteronomy 1:35-38, Numbers 14:30) Israel had just received water from a rock in Rephidim. The people had once again accused Moses of trying to kill them. Despite miracle after miracle, they questioned whether the Lord was even among them. “Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink. And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the LORD?” (Exodus 17:2) “...Is the LORD among us, or not?” (Exodus 17:7) (1 Corinthians 10:1–5)

What should have been a moment of worship became a place of complaint. And in that spiritual vulnerability, the enemy attacked. Amalek seemingly came out of nowhere, at Israel’s most vulnerable moment. Amalek was a desert-dwelling nation, descended from Esau. They were not strangers to Israel, nor were they random aggressors. Again and again throughout Scripture, Amalek represents the flesh—the part of us that rebels against God, resents surrender, and resists obedience. (Galatians 5:16-17, Romans 7:18-25) Israel had just questioned God’s presence—“Is the LORD among us or not?”—and right then, Amalek launched an assault. Their timing wasn’t random. The flesh always fights hardest when faith is weakest.

In 2022, I became a new pastor. It was the great joy and privilege of my life. Shortly thereafter, I was tempted to discontinue a youth camp our church had hosted for many years. It was at this camp, in fact, that I surrendered my life to God as a young man. But in this season, I wanted to quit - not because of the work involved, the financial undertaking it was to the church, or the great amount of time and preparation it required to host camp. No, I wanted to quit because I had little faith that God could use some of the people involved. It is embarrassing to look back on the prideful attitude I had at that moment. But I was convinced I knew better than everyone else. Rather than attempting to work through several differences, my self-centeredness said, “You don’t need them, you are more Spiritual than they are, give in and give it up.”

Praise God for the wise advice of a Godly friend that convinced me not to throw away what God had given me to steward. Over the past few years, God has used this camp to draw many young people to Himself for salvation. Others have come to receive help and healing. These life-changing decisions were made at a camp I wanted to discontinue. My fleshly pride reared its ugly head and nearly convinced me that even God could not use His own people. The flesh always fights hardest when faith is weakest.

When Amalek came, Moses turned to Joshua. “Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said unto Joshua, Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek: to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand.” (Exodus 17:8–9) Israel had no trained soldiers. Joshua was not a trained military leader; he had likely spent his youth as a brickmaker in Egypt. Yet without protest, Joshua obeyed. “So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek.” (Exodus 17:10) There were no excuses. No delay. No strategy meeting or crisis of confidence. He simply obeyed. His courage didn’t come from his experience—it came from Almighty God.

THE HILL AND THE SWORD

While Joshua led the battle in the valley, Moses ascended a hill with the rod of God in his hand. As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed. But when his hands dropped, Amalek gained ground. “And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.” (Exodus 17:11) (1 Timothy 2:8)  So Aaron and Hur came beside him. They found him a seat. Then, one on each side, they held up his arms—steady until the setting of the sun. “And Moses’ hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.” (Exodus 17:12) (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, Galatians 6:2) This is the Scriptural pattern of spiritual victory: prayer, another obedience, and support from the body of Christ. It wasn’t Joshua’s sword, Moses’ rod, or Aaron and Hur’s support system that won the battle. It was God. All the glory belonged to the Lord.

A MEMORIAL AND A MESSAGE

After the battle, God commanded Moses to record what had happened. He was to rehearse it in the ears of Joshua. “And the LORD said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.” (Exodus 17:14) God didn’t want Joshua to remember the fight—He wanted him to remember Who had fought for him.

As a child, I would often wrestle with my dad. I think every six-year-old boy is convinced he can take his “old man” and needs a reminder from time to time that he can’t. Often my dad would say, “Who’s your daddy?” This usually came after tickling us until we screamed like a dying rabbit or tossing us around the living room like a rag doll - Smack! Bam! Wham! “Who’s your daddy?” In a playful way, my dad was reminding us, not about the fight, but who was in charge and who was going to win every time. God wanted Joshua to remember who his “Daddy” was - it was Jehovah God. God would fight for Joshua, and God would win every time!

Moses then built an altar and named it Jehovahnissi: “The Lord is my banner.” “And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it Jehovahnissi: For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.” (Exodus 17:15–16) (Psalm 20:5, 1 Samuel 7:12) That altar marked the moment when a man, who had never led an army, obeyed God, had fearless faith in Him, and witnessed the power of Heaven working through his obedience.

FOUR LESSONS FROM THE FIRST VICTORY

1. Don’t Indulge in Self-Pity Israel was quick to complain when things went wrong: “No food? No water? No army? God has failed us!” But Joshua’s heart said: “No food? No water? No army? No problem! God has never failed us.” We do ourselves no good when we wallow in fear or resentment. God’s provision may still come, but that doesn’t mean He is pleased with our attitude. Don’t confuse the goodness of God in your life as His approval of your poor behavior. Water gushed from the rock, but God was grieved. (Psalm 78:15-22, Lamentations 3:22-23)

2. The Word of the Lord Will Battle Amalek Amalek—the old man, the flesh—will not rest. There will be no ceasefire in this spiritual war. But the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, will always cut through. “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12) (Ephesians 6:17, Matthew 4:1-11)

3. What God Commands, Undertake Immediately Joshua didn’t hesitate. He obeyed the moment the instruction came. This is true faith: not debating, not stalling, but stepping into God’s assignment—even when it feels impossible. “Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.” (John 2:5) (Luke 5:5, James 1:22) God-sized tasks require faith.

4. God Gives Power to Those Who Call on Him Victory in the valley came because of intercession on the hill. Moses couldn’t do it alone. He needed help to keep calling on God. That picture is a reminder to every believer: we are stronger together. When the body of Christ supports each other in prayer, when hands are held up and faith is steady, God works. “Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.” (Jeremiah 33:3) (Matthew 18:19-20, Colossians 4:2)

I recently went through a season of temptation. Every time I stepped foot in a specific location I would be bombarded with the same temptation. “That is simple,” you might say, “stop going to the place you are tempted.” I would usually agree with you. However, this was happening in the new home my wife and I had just purchased. There was no going back. It was a done deal, and the temptations would not stop.

I had two choices: 1. Keep this to myself and attempt to fight alone. I knew this would ultimately lead to failure and sin. 2. Call in backup. Thank God I had the sense to go with option two. I explained the situation to several men of our church, a few pastor friends, and my wife. I asked them to pray that this specific temptation would cease and God would protect our new home from the lies of the enemy. The temptations stopped immediately when they prayed!

Satan wanted to condemn me for being tempted. He wanted to isolate me away from my family and the people of God and make me feel as though I had already sinned. It is not a sin to be tempted - if it is a sin to be tempted, then Jesus was a sinner because He was tempted by Satan. However, it is a sin to dwell upon and act on that temptation.

I was in a battle for my Spiritual life. My hands were weary. I am so grateful for Aarons and Hurs that did not throw me away for being in battle with the enemy, but held up my hands in prayer to God. Victory in the valley came because of intercession on the hill.

THE BATTLE BELONGS TO THE LORD

Who won the battle? Was it Joshua with the sword? Moses with the rod? Aaron and Hur with their support? No. The honor belongs to God alone. He gave the strength. He brought the victory. “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.” (Proverbs 21:31) (2 Chronicles 20:15, Psalm 44:3, Romans 8:37). The same is true for us. Our calling is not to conquer in our own might, but to obey, pray, and trust. The Lord who delivered Israel at Rephidim is still fighting for His people today. And like Joshua, our victories begin with simple, courageous obedience.

Chapter 2 — Signs of Lost Confidence in God

ON THE EDGE OF THE PROMISE

Israel had come to the border of the Promised Land. Behind them was the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock, and the pillar of cloud and fire. In front of them was the land God had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was theirs for the taking. Moses reminded them, “Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it, as the LORD God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged”(Deuteronomy 1:21). God said, “Possess it.” They said, “Let’s assess it first” (Deuteronomy 1:22). They did not move in faith; they balked in fear. Israel had every reason to trust God, yet once again, they doubted Him.

Faith doesn’t stall; faith steps. Israel had seen enough of God’s power to know that giants didn’t matter. Yet the longer they delayed, the bigger the giants grew and the smaller God seemed in their eyes. Delayed obedience weakens trust, and hesitation strengthens fear. What should have been a day of claiming God’s promise became the starting line of forty years of wandering. (Numbers 13:1–3, Hebrews 10:35–36, Proverbs 3:5–6) How did this happen? How did Israel move to a place of fear after watching God work on their behalf? The answer is simple: they lost confidence in God. When a believer loses confidence in God, there will be warning signs. Israel was no exception. Let’s personally consider these warnings lest we too drift into the wilderness of faithlessness.

REFUSAL TO HEAR

The problem wasn’t that Israel didn’t know what God had said — the problem was they didn’t want to hear it. This wasn’t ignorance; it was deliberate. Moses said, “Notwithstanding ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God: and ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us…” (Deuteronomy 1:26-27). God’s voice was clear, but they tuned it out and turned up the voices of fear. When you refuse the truth, you will believe a lie.

Faith grows when we hear and believe the Word of God (Romans 10:17), but when we plug our ears to God’s promises, fear rushes in to fill the silence. The Israelites heard the truth from Joshua and Caleb, but chose to embrace the hopeless report of the ten spies (Numbers 13:31–33). Refusal to hear is the first step toward the death of confidence in God — because when we stop listening to Him, we start listening to anyone and everything else. (Psalm 81:11–13, Hebrews 3:7–8)

REBELLION AGAINST HIS COMMANDMENTS

Moses didn’t soften the truth: “Ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 1:26). Rebellion isn’t always about shaking a fist at heaven. Sometimes it’s cloaked in what we call “caution” or “wisdom,” but at its heart it still says, “I know better than God.” Rebellion doesn’t just resist God; it reverses direction.

The Israelites even went so far as to talk about choosing a new leader and heading back to Egypt (Numbers 14:4). That wasn’t just fear — it was a complete reversal. God had brought them out to bring them in, and they wanted to go back. Rebellion moves you in the exact opposite direction of God’s blessing. When you choose your way over God’s way, you’re declaring you don’t trust Him. (1 Samuel 15:23, John 14:15)

MURMURING

They didn’t just think these things in their hearts — they “murmured in their tents” against the Lord (Deuteronomy 1:27). Murmuring is unbelief with a voice. It takes God’s blessings for granted, rewrites the past to fit our fears, and spreads like wildfire through the camp. The same people who had walked between walls of water on dry ground now grumbled about how much better it would have been to die in Egypt.

(Psalm 106:24–25, Numbers 11:1)

When praise feels awkward and complaint feels natural, you’re in trouble. Murmuring doesn’t just express dissatisfaction; it multiplies it. The more they spoke it, the more they believed it. It poisoned their perspective until the miracles in their midst were invisible, and their hardships were all they could see. Murmuring is never a small sin — it’s an open declaration that you doubt the goodness of the One who delivered you.

(Philippians 2:14-15, 1 Corinthians 10:10)

DISTORTED VIEW OF GOD

They said, “Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us” (Deuteronomy 1:27). Think about that — the same God who parted the Red Sea, who fed them in the desert, who defeated Pharaoh, they now accuse of hating them. Fear always distorts your view of God.

Growing up in northern lower Michigan, I had many recreational opportunities in the outdoors. I love to hunt and chase whitetail deer both with a bow and a firearm. There are few things more beautiful in life than a crisp October morning in a treestand watching the sun peak over the horizon. I love listening to the chickadees fluttering in the trees, watching the leaves fall all around, and seeing the woods come to life as the morning progresses.

To enjoy this morning view, I have to walk into my spot well before daylight. This can be one of the most

terrifying experiences in the outdoors - especially if your trail camera has shown bears or other predators to be in the area the day before. Trekking through the woods with little to no light is an exhilarating experience. In the dark, everything looks and sounds like a bear, wolf, or the Abominable Snow Monster. My adrenal glands pump over a stump that looks like a critter, a stick that looks like a snake, or the flush of a ruffed grouse that will give any grown man a small heart attack. I have walked these areas hundreds of times in the light with no fear, but without light, it seems more ominous. In the dark, fear causes the beautiful forest to look like a dangerous death trap. Fear distorts reality. Fear always distorts your view of God.

A distorted view of God turns every challenge into proof that He’s against you. Instead of seeing the giants as another opportunity to witness His power, they saw them as evidence of His cruelty. If the enemy can convince you that God is against you, you’ll never take the step of faith that proves He is for you. (Jeremiah 29:11, Romans 8:31–32, Nahum 1:7, Psalm 100:5-25, Numbers 11:1)

SELF-CENTERED CIRCUMSTANCES

They said, “The people is greater and taller than we; the cities are great and walled up to heaven… and there we saw the giants” (Deuteronomy 1:28; Numbers 13:31–33). Notice the focus — greater than we, taller than we, stronger than we. Every measurement was made with man as the standard, not God. When you size up your battles by your strength, the giants will always win.

Self-focus skews perspective. Israel forgot the God who had leveled Egypt with plagues, who had split the Red Sea, who had crushed the mightiest army in the world without a sword raised. Now their eyes were locked on their own weakness instead of His strength. If your gaze is on yourself, your faith will shrink; if your gaze is on God, your faith will grow.

(Psalm 27:1, Isaiah 41:10, 2 Corinthians 12:9)

WORRY AND SELF-PITY

“And all the congregation lifted up their voice, and cried; and the people wept that night. And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron: and the whole congregation said unto them, Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt! or would God we had died in this wilderness!” (Numbers 14:1–2). Worry imagines the worst. Self-pity believes the worst has already happened. Worry and self-pity don’t just sap courage — they insult the God who has promised His care. Israel forgot that God had never once failed them. The same God who had brought them out of Egypt was able to bring them into Canaan, but worry and self-pity rewrote the story to make God the villain. If the enemy can get you to dwell on your fears long enough, he can make Egypt look better than the Promised Land.

(Matthew 6:25–34, 1 Peter 5:7, Psalm 55:22, Lamentations 3:21–24)

THE OUTCOME

Their unbelief sealed their fate. “But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness?” (Hebrews 3:17). Unbelief always costs more than obedience. God’s promise didn’t fail — they simply refused to walk into it. Instead of entering the land in days, they wandered in circles for forty years until that generation’s graves marked the desert floor. What they thought was the “safe” choice — avoiding the giants — proved to be the deadliest. They traded milk and honey for manna and funerals. They kept the giants out, but they also kept themselves from God’s best. When you let fear make your decisions, you will always miss the blessings that faith would have claimed.

(Galatians 6:7–8, Proverbs 14:12, Numbers 14:22–23)

THE WAY BACK

The road back to confidence in God isn’t complicated — but it is costly. It demands a heart fully surrendered to Him. Israel had to learn that the same God who led them out was the only One who could lead them in. You can’t get back to confidence IN God without coming back TO God. Coming back to God will require humility, repentance, submission, and remembrance.

Humility – “Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces…” (Numbers 14:5). Humility admits, “Lord, without You I can’t do this.” Pride digs in and defends fear; humility lays it down at the feet of Jesus. You can’t recover confidence in God until you stop pretending you never lost it. (Micah 6:8, James 4:10)

Repentance – Joshua and Caleb stood for truth even when the crowd called for their heads. “Only rebel not ye against the LORD…” (Numbers 14:9). Repentance is more than feeling bad — it’s agreeing with God about your sin and turning from it. It’s choosing His voice over the ten spies EVERY SINGLE TIME. (Acts 3:19, Psalm 51:10) Submission – “…Neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us.” (Numbers 14:9). Submission is bowing to God’s will even when it scares you. You don’t have to understand the path to obey the God who made it. (James 4:7, Proverbs 3:5–6) Obedience does not require explanation.

Rememberance – Finally, remember the Battle is the Lord’s – “If the LORD delight in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it us.”(Numbers 14:8). Victory isn’t about your strength, your plan, or your resources — it’s about His presence. If He’s with you, that’s all you need. (2 Chronicles 20:15, Exodus 14:14) When God’s people humble themselves, repent, submit, and remember His power, their confidence returns, their steps steady, and they start moving forward again. (2 Chronicles 7:14)

Chapter 3 — Wasted Wilderness Wandering — Why?

THE VOICE OF JUDGMENT

The people of Israel cried all night. They had lifted their voices in complaint and accused God of cruelty. They said it would have been better to die in Egypt than to step into the land God had promised them. Then the voice of the Lord broke through their noise: “As truly as I live, saith the LORD, as ye have spoken in mine ears, so will I do to you” (Numbers 14:28). The words must have shaken them to the core. They had spoken of death and defeat, and God said, “So be it.”

When God’s people lost confidence in Him, they were sentenced to the wilderness. Instead of victory, they met wandering. Instead of promise, they met punishment. Their failure was not because God could not bring them in — it was because they would not go in. “So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19).

THEY ASKED FOR IT

The Lord told Israel that He would give them exactly what they had asked for: graves in the wilderness. They cried, “Would God that we had died in this wilderness!” (Numbers 14:2). And God answered, “In this wilderness they shall be consumed, and there they shall die” (Numbers 14:35). Their own words became their sentence. This is the danger of a complaining spirit — it speaks curses into the ears of God. What they called their worst fear became their living reality. Instead of saying, “God is able,” they said, “God has failed us.” And God said, “As you have spoken, so will I do.” How careful we must be with our words, for “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21, Matthew 12:36-37). What you grumble about may be what you get.

DESERT BUT NOT DESERTED

Though Israel murmured, questioned their leaders, and refused to obey God’s plan, God did not abandon His children. He led them to the wilderness and would lead them through it. In their darkest hour and deepest complaint, God still loved and cared for them; but He did not allow them to go into the land He had prepared. Their new life in the desert was harder than the life God had intended. There was food, but not as plentiful or in as great a variety as in Canaan. There was water, but the wilderness was no Jordan. There was shelter in tents, but they did not offer protection like the towns and walled cities of Canaan. God never abandons His children, but the life He intends for them is always better than the life they may choose in self-centeredness. You may feel as though you are in a spiritual wilderness today. You don’t understand where you are or where you

are going spiritually. You seem to be wandering in circles of defeat rather than marching forward in victory. There were clear reasons why Israel was in the wilderness. You may be able to find your way out of the wilderness and back to Canaan, but first, you must discover why you are there and repent!

UNBELIEF

At the heart of their wandering was unbelief. They had seen the Red Sea part, the manna fall, the rock give water, the cloud and fire guide them. Yet when God told them to take the land, they refused. They feared the giants more than they trusted their God. “So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). Unbelief is not a weakness to be excused — it is a sin to be confessed. When we say, “I can’t,” in the face of God’s command, we are really saying, “God won’t.” Faith obeys even when it doesn’t understand. Israel’s unbelief chained them to forty years of wasted wandering, and unbelief still chains us when we refuse to trust God’s Word. (John 3:18, Romans 14:23, Hebrews 11:6) Unbelief doesn’t just doubt God’s power — it denies God’s character.

FINDING FAULT WITH GOD’S PLAN

The Israelites said, “Wherefore hath the LORD brought us unto this land, to fall by the sword, that our wives and our children should be a prey?” (Numbers 14:3). They looked at the promise of God and called it a death trap. They looked at His love and called it hatred. Instead of trusting His plan, they slandered His heart. In 2019, my wife and I received the news that we would not be able to have biological children. We desired to start a family, but after several years of unsuccessful family planning and medical tests showed I was sterile. It was the first time as an adult that something was wrong, and there was nothing I could do to fix it. To say we were disappointed would be an understatement. My wife was devastated.

It was at this all-time low that questions began to creep in. Why would God allow others to have children but not us? Had we done something wrong? Was God punishing us for unconfessed sin? These questions and lies from the enemy could have turned to bitterness toward God and fault-finding in His plan.

As I am writing this paragraph, seated at my kitchen table, I am watching my three oldest children play in the living room. They are playing loud enough to wake up our youngest little girl, Ella, who is already down for the night. Looking back, I can see God had not abandoned us, nor was He punishing us - He was working His plan. His plan involved the wonderful adoption journey of our oldest son, Tucker, and the miraculous conception of our daughter, Quinn, weeks before Tucker arrived. God’s plan involved a season of waiting on Him. If we could do it all over again, we would choose God’s way every time. The fear of being childless could have caused us to find fault in God and His character. He taught us an invaluable lesson - His plan is always best. When we lose confidence in God, we will begin to accuse Him. We twist His goodness into cruelty, His blessings into burdens. Like Israel, we may say with our mouths, “The Lord is good,” but in our hearts we whisper, “Does He really care about me?” And nothing dishonors God more than accusing Him of being unfaithful. (Jeremiah 29:11, Romans 8:31–32, Nahum 1:7) Fear always finds fault with God’s plan.

REBELLION AND MURMURING

Unbelief soon gave birth to rebellion. The people said one to another, “Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt” (Numbers 14:4). They weren’t just afraid — they were ready to replace God’s appointed leader, reject His command, and run back to slavery. Moses said plainly, “Ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 1:26). Their rebellion was fueled by murmuring. Scripture says, “Notwithstanding ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God: and ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us…” (Deuteronomy 1:26-27). Murmuring spreads like a disease. It magnifies giants, minimizes God, and multiplies fear. No wonder Paul warns, “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10:10). Complaining isn’t harmless — it is unbelief with a voice.

DISTORTED VIEW OF GOD

The saddest words may be these: “Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us” (Deuteronomy 1:27). Imagine — after all God had done, after plagues, Passover, and parting seas, they accused Him of hatred.

Satan desires for us to view God as an unjust disciplinarian. He feeds the lie that God’s love is like the imperfect love of an abusive father or overbearing mother. He tricks us into viewing God through our circumstances rather than seeing our circumstances through God. The only way to have a proper view of God is to view Him through the lens of His Word and Spirit. The Spirit will show us the truth of our circumstances and provide a proper view of God. “Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.” (John 16:13)

Fear distorts our view of God. Instead of seeing challenges as opportunities for God’s glory, they saw them as evidence of His cruelty. But the truth was the opposite — His plan was their life, their freedom, their blessing. When you lose confidence in God, you will misinterpret His love. (Romans 8:35–39, Psalm 100:5, James 1:17) You cannot have a distorted view of God and a proper view of your circumstances, hardship, relationships, or life’s purpose.

THE OUTCOME

Because of their unbelief and rebellion, God declared that generation would not enter the land. “Doubtless ye shall not come into the land, concerning which I sware to make you dwell therein, save Caleb… and Joshua” (Numbers 14:30). Their children, whom they claimed would die by the sword, would live to inherit what they forfeited. But for them, forty years of wandering awaited until every unbelieving voice was silenced in death. This was not God’s failure — it was theirs. His promise was still true. His power was still sufficient. But their unbelief wasted their opportunity for Canaan. What could have been a journey of victory became a graveyard of wasted years. (Hebrews 3:17–19, Galatians 6:7–8, James 1:15) Unbelief always costs more than obedience.

THE WAY BACK

And yet, even in judgment, there was a way back. Joshua and Caleb pleaded with the people: “Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not” (Numbers 14:9). The answer was simple — humility, repentance, submission, and remembering the Lord’s presence.

This is still the path today. When we find ourselves wandering, wasting, and weary, the way back is the same: bow low in humility, confess unbelief, submit to His Word, and remember that the battle belongs to the Lord. The same God who brought Israel out of Egypt is able to carry us into victory if we will only trust Him. (2 Chronicles 7:14, Acts 3:19, James 4:7, Jeremiah 33:3) Your wilderness is wasted only if you stay there. Meditative Thoughts:

Chapter 4 — Joshua’s Encouragement

A HEAVY ASSIGNMENT

“But Joshua the son of Nun, which standeth before thee, he shall go in thither: encourage him: for he shall cause Israel to inherit it” (Deuteronomy 1:38). God gave Joshua an enormous task—to lead an unleadable people into an unconquerable land. He had seen Moses’ anguish, his grief, his frustration. Joshua knew what it cost to lead Israel. He wasn’t stepping into something easy. He was stepping into something humanly impossible. God knew he would need more than skill or strategy—he would need encouragement.

Encouragement is never a small thing when the task before us is overwhelming. Joshua would face giants, walled cities, and a nation prone to rebellion. Yet God arranged a network of encouragement—divine, spiritual, and personal—to steady him for the road ahead. (Joshua 1:1-5, Psalm 27:1, Hebrews 13:5-6)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD

The first and greatest encourager in Joshua’s life was God Himself. “Now after the death of Moses… the LORD spake unto Joshua” (Joshua 1:1). When God gives an assignment, He never abandons His servant. Joshua didn’t have to invent his mission or fuel his courage alone—God Himself spoke words of strength into his heart. That truth still stands. When you are walking in obedience to God’s will, you can expect His presence, His care, and His encouragement. He is not a distant commander sending you into danger without aid—He is the Captain of your salvation who goes with you into every battle. (Deuteronomy 31:6, Isaiah 41:10, Matthew 28:20)

ENCOURAGED BY MOSES

Moses had been Joshua’s leader, mentor, and commander. From the very beginning, God told Moses: “Encourage him: for he shall cause Israel to inherit it” (Deuteronomy 1:38). Moses had seen Joshua’s faith in the wilderness, and he knew this young man was God’s chosen successor. His charge wasn’t optional—it was essential.

There is no substitute for the peace that comes when a godly leader looks you in the eye and says, “By God’s grace, you can do this.” When I became a new young pastor, I was encouraged by many fellow pastors, servants of God, and church members in a similar way. This instilled such confidence in me. However, I was shocked by how many others “encouraged” me with advice such as, “Just you wait, now you’ll see what it’s really like to be in ministry,” “You’re only 27? Your excitement will wear off soon enough,” and “Oh, the honeymoon will be over soon.” This was obviously not helpful, life-giving, or encouraging. I knew there would be difficulties ahead. I knew there was much I didn’t know and had not experienced, but I was excited to be a pastor! I remind myself often not to “encourage” others in this way. It is not encouraging; it is disheartening. Moses encouraged Joshua by reminding him that the Lord would be with him, and that was all he would need.

Moses, who had endured the murmuring and rebellion of Israel, told Joshua to go forward with confidence. And when Moses laid his hands on him, it was as if God Himself was placing His approval on Joshua’s call. (Numbers 27:18-23, 1 Timothy 4:14)

ENCOURAGED BY ELEAZAR

Joshua also received encouragement from Eleazar the priest. Numbers 27 records that Moses brought Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation to give him a charge in their sight. The high priest would become Joshua’s associate in leadership, a spiritual counselor pointing him toward God’s wisdom and direction.

Encouragement flows not only from God and from leaders but also from spiritual mentors who walk beside us. Eleazar’s presence reminded Joshua that he was not leading alone. God had provided godly counsel, spiritual reinforcement, and intercession. Joshua was encouraged by prophet, priest, and king - Moses, Eleazar, and God. The same is true for us: God often places encouragers in our path if we are humble enough to listen. (Proverbs 11:14, Hebrews 13:17)

ENCOURAGED BY VICTORIES

One of the ways God strengthened Joshua was by reminding him of what he had already seen. He had stood on the battlefield when Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, fell. “Thine eyes have seen all that the LORD your God hath done… so shall the LORD do” (Deuteronomy 3:21).

When the future looks impossible, look back at God’s past faithfulness. Joshua’s encouragement wasn’t only in the promise of what God would do—it was in the memory of what God had already done. Every past victory was a pledge of future triumph. (1 Samuel 17:37, Psalm 77:11-12, Philippians 1:6)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PRESENCE

Joshua was told again and again: “The LORD your God he shall fight for you” (Deuteronomy 3:22). When God sends you into battle, He does not leave you to fight alone. His presence is both the guarantee of victory and the cure for fear.

David would later stand before Goliath with the same confidence, declaring that the battle is the Lord’s. Joshua could march forward with courage, not because he was mighty, but because his God was. And the same God who fought for Joshua fights for His children today. (Exodus 14:14, 1 Samuel 17:47, Romans 8:31)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PROMISES

God’s promise of the land was not new—it stretched back to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But now it was Joshua’s turn to believe it personally. Moses was told: “Charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people” (Deuteronomy 3:28). God’s promises are never “if” but “when.” Joshua’s encouragement was anchored in the certainty of God’s Word. What God has spoken, He would do. Faith finds its courage not in what we see but in what He has said. (Romans 4:20-21, 2 Corinthians 1:20, Hebrews 10:23)

ENCOURAGED BY SONGS

Moses even left behind a song to be sung in Israel as a witness (Deuteronomy 32). Deuteronomy 31 tells us that God commanded Moses to teach it to the people so that when trouble came, the melody of truth would echo in their hearts.

Songs have a unique way of carrying truth into the soul. They remind us of God’s character, His works, and His promises. That’s why Scripture tells us to speak to ourselves “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.” Joshua’s encouragement included not only commands and victories but also songs of faith that would outlast the darkest days. (Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16, Psalm 42:8)

ENCOURAGED BY WISDOM

After Moses’ death, the people wept for thirty days, asking, “What are we going to do without Moses?” But the Lord had already provided. “And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him” (Deuteronomy 34:9).

God never leaves His people leaderless or powerless. Joshua’s encouragement was in knowing that God had given him divine wisdom for the task. That same wisdom is offered freely to every believer who asks in faith. (James 1:5, Isaiah 11:2, Colossians 1:9)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PROSPERITY

When Joshua finally stepped into leadership, God gave him this promise: “Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you” (Joshua 1:3). No enemy, no obstacle, no limitation could stand in the way of God’s plan.

Encouragement comes when we realize that success in God’s work is not based on our ability but on His faithfulness. Yielded hearts, Spirit-filled lives, and obedient steps will always find the path open and the victory sure. (Joshua 1:5, Proverbs 16:3, Romans 8:37)

JOSHUA’S QUIET CONFIDENCE

Joshua didn’t seize leadership with fanfare. He simply issued a calm directive: “Prepare you victuals; for within three days ye shall pass over this Jordan” (Joshua 1:11). No drama. No delay. Just steady faith in God. Joshua was ready to move with God, and because of his encouragement in the Lord, he did in a few days what Moses could not in forty years. Encouragement turns fearful hesitation into faithful action. (Psalm 31:24, Isaiah 40:31, 2 Timothy 1:7)

Chapter 5 — Spiritual Battles

THE BATTLES WE FACE

The psalmist sang, “To him which smote great kings: for his mercy endureth for ever: Sihon king of the Amorites… and Og the king of Bashan” (Psalm 136:17-20). Israel’s history is marked by battles, and Joshua’s life was no exception. Some of these conflicts were against nations with armies and fortresses, but others pointed to greater spiritual realities—the ongoing war every believer faces in their soul. These stories are not just Israel’s history; they are portraits of our spiritual battles today.

The enemies Joshua fought still represent the enemies we must face—our flesh, our besetting sins, and the lies of false religion. Just like Israel, if we refuse the fight, the consequence is wandering in the wilderness of divided loyalties and Spiritual dryness. (Romans 15:4, 1 Corinthians 10:11)

THE BATTLE WITH THE FLESH

The first time Joshua ever led an army, it was against Amalek in Rephidim (Exodus 17). Amalek was relentless, attacking Israel when they were weary and unprepared. Throughout Scripture, Amalek becomes a symbol of the flesh—the sinful nature that wages war against the Spirit of God within us. Paul wrote, “For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). Amalek is alive and well today - the struggle hasn’t changed. The flesh whispers when you are tired, discouraged, or spiritually dry. It surfaces in anger when truth cuts too close to the heart. It urges comfort when obedience demands sacrifice. It resists prayer, avoids Scripture, and clings to pride. Like Amalek, the flesh never negotiates and never rests—it must be fought daily. If we do not, it will gain ground in our lives. (Romans 7:18–25, Ephesians 6:10–12)

The flesh is always stronger when faith grows weaker. Amalek came after Israel the moment they questioned, “Is the LORD among us, or not?” (Exodus 17:7). The same is true for us. Doubt feeds the flesh. Faith defeats it. (1 Corinthians 9:27, James 4:7)

THE FIGHT AGAINST BESETTING SIN

Later, Israel faced Sihon, king of the Amorites (Deuteronomy 2:30–33). At first glance, Sihon seemed just another Canaanite king, but his territory controlled the road Israel needed to pass through. Sihon represents the besetting sins that block our way forward with God—the habits, indulgences, or attitudes that keep us wandering instead of progressing.

A besetting sin can be hidden, respectable, even excused. Maybe it’s a sharp tongue you justify as “just being honest.” Maybe it’s a secret indulgence you think no one sees. Maybe it’s bitterness that you carry because of what someone else has done. Maybe it’s anxiety, dishonesty, infidelity, or unholy living. Left unchecked, these sins claim territory in your heart and prevent you from moving forward in obedience. “Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). Moses wanted to live peaceably with Sihon and skirt around him. God wanted Sihon destroyed. “And I sent messengers out of the wilderness of Kedemoth unto Sihon king of Heshbon with words of peace, saying, Let me pass through thy land: I will go along by the high way, I will neither turn unto the right hand nor to the left. But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him: for the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand, as appeareth this day.”

(Deuteronomy 2:26-27, 30)

Israel could not enter their inheritance until Sihon was defeated. Neither can we walk in victory while excusing sin that God has already told us to surrender. God does not make peace with what keeps His children enslaved. (Romans 6:12–14, Colossians 3:5–10) You cannot keep Sihon and take Canaan at the same time. The fight must be faced, and victory only comes through God’s power. (2 Corinthians 7:1, 1 John 1:9)

THE LAST GIANT

Then came Og, king of Bashan, whose bedstead was made of iron (Deuteronomy 3:11). Og was a giant, and his kingdom represented intimidation. If Sihon represents the sins we coddle, Og represents the strongholds we fear—those towering lies and false beliefs that make us think victory is impossible.

For Israel, Og’s fortress was fearsome. For us, Og looks like false teaching, spiritual deception, or deeply rooted sin that feels unbreakable. Satan still uses giants to make God’s people feel small. Jesus warned of wolves in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15). Paul warned of philosophies and traditions that spoil through deceit (Colossians 2:8). John warned of many false spirits gone out into the world (1 John 4:1).

False religion and deception are not minor skirmishes; they are giants. They enslave hearts, corrupt truth, and turn worship away from the living God. Just as Joshua led Israel to slay Og, believers must confront lies with the truth of God’s Word. “Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32). No giant is greater than God. The same Lord who felled Og is the Lord who still topples strongholds today.

(2 Corinthians 10:3–5, Isaiah 54:17)

THE CONSEQUENCE OF REFUSING THE FIGHT

God warned His people, “If ye will not drive out the inhabitants of the land… those which ye let remain shall be pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides” (Numbers 33:55). Every enemy Israel spared came back to haunt them. Every compromise grew into corruption. When we refuse to fight the flesh, the besetting sin, or the giants of deception, the consequences are the same. Wandering replaces victory. Compromise replaces courage. Sin, left unchallenged, will not leave us alone— it will control us. Samson learned it in Delilah’s lap. Solomon learned it in his divided heart. Demas learned it in his love for this present world. (Judges 16:19–21, 1 Kings 11:4, 2 Timothy 4:10) What you refuse to fight today will rule you tomorrow. God’s warning is not to discourage, but to protect. The same God who promised victory to Joshua has promised us His Spirit, His Word, and His presence in every battle.

(Romans 8:37, Ephesians 6:17–18)

THE WAY TO VICTORY

Joshua’s victories remind us that battles are not won in our strength but in God’s. Amalek fell when Moses’ hands were lifted in prayer. Sihon fell when Israel trusted God’s word instead of skirting around the problem. Og fell because God went before them. Not one victory was secured by human might.

Our victory, too, comes by the Spirit. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). The same Lord who gave Joshua victory gives His people power today through the Word, through prayer, and through faith. The battle is real, but so is victory through Christ.

Chapter 6 — The Cost of Compromise

THE REQUEST AT THE JORDAN

Israel stood at the edge of promise. The land flowed with milk and honey, but before crossing Jordan, two and a half tribes hesitated. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh looked around and thought, “This land east of Jordan is good enough. Why fight further when we could settle here?” Scripture records their request: “The children of Reuben and the children of Gad had a very great multitude of cattle: and when they saw the land of Jazer, and the land of Gilead, that, behold, the place was a place for cattle; the children of Gad and the children of Reuben came and spake unto Moses… saying, The country which the LORD smote before the congregation of Israel, is a land for cattle, and thy servants have cattle: Wherefore, said they, if we have found grace in thy sight, let this land be given unto thy servants for a possession, and bring us not over Jordan” (Numbers 32:1–5). At first glance, their reasoning seemed harmless, even practical. The land fit their needs. But compromise always looks reasonable at the beginning. It avoids the harder path and settles for what is close, but not best. God does not ask us to choose what looks right from our human perspective - He asks us to obey His simple commands. Sadly, for Reuben, Gad, and Menasseh, compromise always carries a cost.

(Deuteronomy 11:10–12; Hebrews 10:38)

THE REASON FOR COMPROMISE

The tribes’ reasoning was rooted in possessions and convenience. They had cattle, and the land was good for cattle. But the call of God was not to settle for what pleased the eye. It was to claim what He had promised. Their logic revealed a divided heart—looking at life through the lens of ease rather than obedience. This is where compromise begins for us, too. We weigh God’s will against our desires. We measure faith by convenience. We choose the job that pays more instead of the path God called us to walk. We stay silent when speaking the truth might cost us. We quench the Spirit’s leading when His command doesn’t suit our fancy. Like Reuben and Gad, we let possessions, comfort, or security become the deciding factor. Compromise always chooses the easier side of Jordan. (Matthew 6:24; 1 John 2:15-17)

DISCOURAGEMENT TO THE FAITHFUL

Moses’ response was sharp: “Wherefore discourage ye the heart of the children of Israel from going over into the land which the LORD hath given them?” (Numbers 32:7). Their compromise was not private—it discouraged the faith of the whole nation. Those ready to fight now wondered if the fight was worth it. That’s the poison

of compromise—it never stays personal. Parents who compromise discourage their children’s zeal. Leaders who compromise weaken their followers’ faith. Christians who choose comfort over obedience make it harder for others to keep pressing forward. Compromise is contagious, and its ripple effect often lasts for generations. (Romans 14:7; Hebrews 12:15)

ANGERING THE ALMIGHTY

Moses did not soften the warning: “Behold, ye are risen up in your fathers’ stead, an increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel” (Numbers 32:14). Their compromise was not a harmless choice—it provoked God’s anger. It echoed the unbelief of Kadesh-barnea, when fear turned the nation back into the wilderness. When God calls us forward and we refuse, it is rebellion. He had promised Canaan, sworn to give them victory, and displayed His power at every turn. To stop short was to call God unfaithful. Compromise is never neutral—it insults the character of God. (Deuteronomy 9:23; Hebrews 3:17–19)

You may be wondering, “What is the cost of compromise?” Consider the price Reuben, Gad, and Menasseh paid.

DIVIDED LOYALTIES AND AFFECTIONS

Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh promised Moses they would fight with their brethren but return to their own land afterward. Their bodies would cross the Jordan, but their hearts would stay behind. Their loyalty was divided. This is the cost of compromise—it creates a faith that goes halfway, a devotion that cannot last. Jesus warned, “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). Half-hearted discipleship is not discipleship at all. Listen to Jesus’ description of a true follower of Him. “If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. And whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple. So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple.” (Luke 14:26-27,33) Carefully reread these verses. Is that you? Divided affections make it impossible to love God fully. The man who settles for Jordan’s edge will never know Jordan’s joy.

(James 1:8; Matthew 6:33)

FIRST TO FALL

Centuries later, when enemies swept into Israel, who were the first to fall? Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh. The land they thought was safer proved to be most vulnerable. Their compromise made them the first casualties.

This is the sobering lesson: what we think will protect us often destroys us. The easier path becomes the weaker path. Those who choose comfort over obedience forfeit the protection of God’s promise. Compromise may feel like safety in the short term, but it always exposes us in the long run. (1 Peter 5:8; Galatians 6:7–8)

THE FINAL WARNING

Moses concluded with a solemn reminder: “Be sure your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23). He wasn’t talking to idolaters or pagans—he was warning God’s people who wanted to settle short of His promise. The wilderness had already proven what unbelief costs, yet here was a new generation standing at the same dangerous place. Every believer will face this temptation: to take the land of convenience instead of the land of promise. But God has not called us to settle east of Jordan. He has called us to trust Him, follow Him, and fight forward into His best. (Philippians 3:13–14; Hebrews 12:1–2)

Chapter 7 — The Ark of God

TIME TO CROSS

It was time. After years of wandering, Israel stood at the edge of the Jordan River, ready to enter the land God had promised. Picture it: Joshua rises early, the morning sun spreading over the camp, the sound of cattle stirring, pots clanking, children yawning, and tents opening. The day had finally come to possess what God had promised. “And Joshua rose early in the morning; and they removed from Shittim, and came to Jordan, he and all the children of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.” (Joshua 3:1) But this would not be like any other march. The officers went through the camp with specific instructions: “When ye see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, and the priests the Levites bearing it, then ye shall remove from your place, and go after it.” (Joshua 3:3) This was a new way forward. No murmuring or doubting, no shouts of war or battle horns—just a people moving with eyes fixed on the Ark. (Deuteronomy 31:7-8, Hebrews 11:8)

A NEW WAY

Israel had come to know God through miraculous signs: pillars of cloud and fire, manna from heaven, water from the rock. But now God would lead them in a deeper way— through His presence represented by the Ark. Where He went, they would go. What He said, they would do. Joshua would not tolerate doubt or murmuring; the time for hesitation had ended. “Choose you this day whom ye will serve… but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” (Joshua 24:15)

God’s ways are never what we expect. (Isaiah 55:8-9) An army on the verge of invasion usually moves with noise, intimidation, and force. Yet this crossing was silent—a nation moving together in faith. No pomp, no fanfare— only a people obeying divine direction. And nothing would stand in their way. (Psalm 33:16-18)

THE ARK – GOD’S PRESENCE

The Ark represented the very presence of God among His people. Joshua told them, “Hereby ye shall know that the living God is among you, and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites… Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth passeth over before you into Jordan.” (Joshua 3:10-11) What confidence this gave! The Ark meant God was with them. Today, our confidence is greater still—not only is God with us, He is in us. Jesus promised, “I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you… ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you.” (John 14:18-20) His Spirit abides forever. The Ark was a symbol; Christ is the reality. (Romans 8:9, Colossians 1:27)

THE ARK – GOD’S PROMISES

Every glance at the Ark reminded Israel of covenant promises. God had told Abraham: He would show him a land, make his name great, bless his seed, and through him bless all nations. (Genesis 12:1-3) That promise pointed ultimately to Christ, through whom salvation would come.

Peter reminds us that believers today are also heirs of promises: “Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature.” (2 Peter 1:4) The Ark reminded Israel of God’s faithfulness; the cross reminds us of ours. (Hebrews 10:23, 2 Corinthians 1:20)

THE ARK – GOD’S POWER

Israel could not conquer Canaan in their own strength. Left to themselves, they would falter. But the Ark declared God’s enabling power. What He begins, He completes. What He commands, He supplies. He gives daily bread for strength, wisdom for confusion, and makes a way when none can be seen. “Now the God of peace… make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight.” (Hebrews 13:20-21) We are not called to do His bidding alone. God’s power equips His people. (Philippians 2:13, Isaiah 41:10)

THE ARK – ITS CONTENTS

Inside the Ark were three sacred items, each a testimony of God’s work. “…the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant.” (Hebrews 9:4) The manna reminded Israel of God’s provision. For forty years they had eaten heaven’s bread. Each meal declared that He sustains His people daily. (Exodus 16:31-35, Matthew 6:11) Aaron’s rod testified of God’s deliverance and authority. It was the rod that struck Egypt’s waters, called forth plagues, and later budded as a sign against rebellion. God had the power not only to redeem from bondage but also to unite His people under His order. (Exodus 7:19, Numbers 17:8-10) The tablets of stone bore God’s covenant, pointing forward to the greater covenant in Christ, where His law is written on hearts and sins remembered no more. (Exodus 25:16, Hebrews 10:16-17) Each article inside the Ark told a story: God provides, God delivers, God covenants.

THE ARK – A PATTERN FOR LIFE

The people were told, “When ye see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God… then ye shall remove from your place, and go after it.” (Joshua 3:3) The principle is clear: when God moves, we move; when He stops, we stop. A life of victory is a life lived in step with Him. (Psalm 37:23, Galatians 5:25) How do we follow Him today? By walking with Him in prayer, seeking His face, listening for His voice, and watching His activity around us. The Scriptures must be our standard of life—not just a book on the shelf, but the living Word shaping every choice. (Psalm 119:105, James 1:22)

Undying devotion to His will is the only fitting response. Nothing in our heart, home, career, or church is off-limits to His call. Where He leads, we must follow. (Luke 9:23, Romans 12:1-2)

Chapter 8 — Joshua – A Portrait of Christ

A GREATER JOSHUA

Stephen, standing before the Sanhedrin, reminded Israel of their own history: “Our fathers had the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness… which also our fathers that came after brought in with Jesus (Joshua - Jehoshua) into the possession of the Gentiles, whom God drave out before the face of our fathers, unto the days of David” (Acts 7:44–45). The Bible uses the name Jesus here, but it refers to Joshua—the servant of Moses who led God’s people into the Promised Land. Even in this small detail, Scripture ties the two names together. Joshua was the leader who brought Israel into Canaan, but Jesus is the Captain who brings His people into eternal rest.

God loved His Son so much, He gave us the Old Testament as a photo album, full of pictures of His precious Son Jesus Christ. Joshua’s life, battles, and leadership were never just about Joshua. They pointed forward. They were a shadow of something greater, a portrait of Christ Himself. Every page of his story whispers, “There is another coming—greater, perfect, victorious.” In this chapter, we will note the undeniable similarities between Jesus and Joshua.

APPOINTED BY GOD

Joshua did not volunteer for leadership; he was appointed. God told Moses, “Take thee Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the spirit, and lay thine hand upon him” (Numbers 27:18). Joshua’s authority was not self-made—it was given from heaven.

In the same way, Christ was appointed by God as the Saviour of the world. Isaiah prophesied, “Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth” (Isaiah 42:1). Revelation 3 calls Jesus “...the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.” This divine appointment of His Son pleased God. At Jesus’ baptism, the heavens opened and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). When God appoints, no man can overthrow. Joshua’s commission was secure because God had spoken. Christ’s mission was certain because God had decreed it from eternity. As Joshua was called to lead Israel into a land of promise, Christ was appointed to lead His people into eternal life. (John 6:38–40, Hebrews 5:5–6)

IMPORTANCE OF THE NAME

Joshua’s original name was not Joshua, but Oshea (Hosea). “These are the names of the men which Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua.” (Numbers 13:16) Joshua’s original name, Oshea, carries the meaning “a prayer for Salvation” Joshua’s new name, given to him by Moses, means Jehovah saves. What a powerful picture in the changing of a name from “a prayer for Salvation, to Jehovah is salvation. Joshua’s name change answered the question all men ask, in one simple name - Jesus. The name Joshua in Hebrew is Yehoshua, meaning “Jehovah is salvation.” In Greek, that same name is rendered Iesous—Jesus. The very name Joshua bore is the name above every name.

When the angel appeared to Joseph, he said of Mary’s child: “Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Joshua saved Israel from wandering and brought them into Canaan. Jesus saves sinners from wrath and brings them into glory. But the similarity in the names of these men goes even deeper. Just as Oshea (Joshua) was given a new name, Jesus Christ will also be given a new name. “His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns; and he had a name written, that no man knew, but he himself.” (Revelation 19:12)

This is no accident. God designed Joshua’s life and name as a living pointer to Christ. Every time Israel called their leader’s name, they were declaring the truth of salvation. And every time we whisper the name of Jesus in prayer, we are confessing that salvation belongs to the Lord. (Acts 4:12, Philippians 2:9–11) The salvation Joshua offered to Israel was temporary, but Salvation in Jesus Christ is eternal. Joshua offered salvation only to the current nation of Israel, but Jesus offers salvation to all the world!

SUCCESSOR TO MOSES

Moses, the lawgiver, could not bring Israel into the Promised Land. He could see it, he could preach it, but he could not lead them in. That task fell to Joshua. “The LORD said unto Moses, Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers… but Joshua he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land” (Deuteronomy 31:16, 23). This is more than history; it is theology. The law, referred to as “Moses” by the Jews, could never bring us into God’s rest. It could reveal our sin but it could not give life. Paul declared, “If there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law” (Galatians 3:21). But it is Christ, the greater Joshua, who accomplishes what Moses never could. “For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). The law points to our need, but only Jesus brings us home. Joshua succeeded Moses, not because Moses failed, but because God was showing that His law must give way to His grace.

(Romans 8:3–4, Hebrews 4:8–10)

LEADER AND DELIVERER WHO FOLLOWED GOD

Joshua was a leader and deliverer who followed God. He led the people across Jordan, conquered Jericho, divided the inheritance, and gave rest to the tribes. However, Joshua did not lead the people to accomplish his own mission, he led Israel as he personally followed God. Joshua’s leadership ultimately led to the deliverance of his followers. His leadership was steady, his obedience to God’s leading resolute. When many turned to idols, Joshua declared, “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Yet Joshua’s victories were temporary. The people strayed again and again. Their rest was incomplete. Hebrews 4:8 says, “If Jesus [Joshua] had given them rest, then would he not afterward have spoken of another day.”

Jesus, too, was a Leader and Deliverer Who followed God. When Jesus came to earth, He did only what the Father told Him to do. Jesus perfectly followed His Leader. “Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise.” (John 5:19) Jesus led by following the Father. He is the faithful Leader who never falters, the Deliverer who never loses one of His own. Joshua delivered Israel from their enemies; Christ delivered His church from sin, death, and the grave. (Colossians 1:13–14, 1 Corinthians 15:57)

WARRIOR WHO CONQUERS EVERY ENEMY

Joshua faced Amalek, Jericho, Ai, and countless Canaanite and Amorite kings. One by one, they fell. Joshua clung to the promise from God that no enemy would stand against him. “There shall not any man be able to stand before thee all the days of thy life....” (Joshua 1:5) God was faithful to His promise. Joshua conquered his enemies. So too with Christ; He is the Ultimate Warrior that crushed His enemies. At the cross, it looked like defeat. The spear pierced Him, the grave seemingly swallowed Him, the enemy rejoiced. But on the third day, He rose triumphant. Paul declared, “Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). Every enemy bows before Jesus. Joshua put his foot on the necks of five kings (Joshua 10:24) but Christ has crushed the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Death is defeated, hell is broken, sin is conquered. “Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57). (Romans 8:37, Revelation 19:11–16)

PROPHET WHO SPEAKS THE WORD OF GOD

Joshua functioned as a prophet to Israel several times. He received a word from God and proclaimed it to His people. (Joshua 3:9) Jesus was a prophet in Israel. “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” (John 1:18) He not only spoke on behalf of God; he spoke as God. Notice the power in His words. “Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye? They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am he. And Judas also, which betrayed him, stood with them. As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground.” (John 18:4-6)

VICTOR WHO SHARES HIS INHERITANCE

After leading Israel to complete victory in Canaan, Joshua divided the land among the people.

He did not usurp greedy authority over them, claiming the land all for himself, setting himself over them as king. Rather, he divided the land of promise among his followers. (Joshua 21:43-45) Jesus, after conquering death, shared victory and peace with His people as their inheritance. (Galatians 3:26-29) He also has promised an eternal home with him and made us joint-heirs of His inheritance with Him!

THE TRUE AND GREATER JOSHUA

Joshua was a portrait. Jesus is the Person. Joshua led Israel into Canaan; Jesus leads us into the New Jerusalem. Joshua fought nations; Jesus fought the hosts of hell. Joshua gave a temporary rest; Jesus gives eternal life. Joshua’s name meant “Jehovah is salvation”; Jesus is salvation. The Old Testament closes with longing. The New Testament opens with fulfillment. What Joshua began, Jesus Christ completes. He is the Captain of our salvation (Hebrews 2:10), the Leader who never fails, the Victor who never loses, the Deliverer who never forsakes.

Chapter 9 — Jordan Memorials

STEPPING ONTO DRY GROUND

The Jordan River was at flood stage when Israel arrived at its banks. To the human eye, it was an impossible crossing. Yet when the priests’ feet touched the water, “the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap… and the people passed over right against Jericho” (Joshua 3:16). What God had done at the Red Sea for their parents, He now did again for this new generation.

As the entire nation walked across on dry ground, God told Joshua to mark the moment. “Take you twelve men out of the people, out of every tribe a man, and command ye them, saying, Take you hence out of the midst of Jordan, out of the place where the priests’ feet stood firm, twelve stones, and ye shall carry them over with you” (Joshua 4:2–3). God wanted His people to never forget this day.

Faith easily fades when God is not remembered. Miracles lose their weight when they are not rehearsed. God knew His people would need a memorial they could point to and say, “This is where God proved Himself faithful.” (Psalm 77:11–12, Deuteronomy 6:12)

RECORDING GOD’S WORK

Joshua obeyed God’s command immediately. He chose twelve men, one from each tribe, and had them carry a stone out of the river. The stones weren’t polished, carved, or decorated. They were ordinary, but their placement gave them meaning. “Those twelve stones, which they took out of Jordan, did Joshua pitch in Gilgal. And he spake unto the children of Israel, saying, When your children shall ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean these stones? Then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land.” (Joshua 4:20–22). The purpose of the memorial was not art but memory. It was a visible testimony that pointed to an invisible God. Parents would one day stand at Gilgal with their children, look at those stones, and retell the story. Faith would not die with one generation—it would pass on. (Psalm 78:4–7, Joel 1:3)

We often underestimate the importance of writing down, recording, and remembering what God has done for us. Journaling our burdens, testimonies, and answered prayers can serve as our memorial stones. Forgetting is easy. Recording is remembering. (Exodus 17:14, Malachi 3:16)

STONES ON THE BANK

The stones on the bank stood as a public witness. They told every Israelite, and even their enemies, that God had brought His people into the land by His power, not their own. It wasn’t their strategy, their numbers, or their might—it was His hand. The stones also marked the beginning of something new. For forty years they had wandered in circles, waiting for graves in the wilderness. Now they were in the land of promise. Each stone was a declaration: “We are here because God brought us here.” (Psalm 126:3, Isaiah 43:18–19)

In our own lives, there ought to be places where we can look back and say, “That’s where God brought me through. That’s where I trusted Him, and He proved Himself faithful.” These public testimonies are not for pride, but for praise. They remind us, and they tell others, that the God who parted Jordan is still the God who delivers today. (Psalm 40:1–3, 1 Peter 2:9)

STONES IN THE RIVER

But there was a second memorial, less visible, yet just as important. Joshua himself took twelve stones and set them up in the very midst of Jordan, “in the place where the feet of the priests which bare the ark of the covenant stood” (Joshua 4:9). These stones were not carried to the bank. They stayed hidden beneath the water. Why two memorials? One was seen by all; the other was seen only by God. The stones in the river were a personal act of devotion, a private acknowledgment that God had been faithful. These stones would only appear when the river ran dry, but God knew they were there.

So it is with us. Some testimonies are public—stories we share, songs we sing, memorials others can see. But others are quiet, personal, and known only to God. These hidden memorials are the private prayers of gratitude, the altars built in the quiet moments when no one is watching. These private memorials are reminders during physical, emotional, and spiritual drought that God is faithful. Often, private memorials are only remembered in difficulty, but it is then they are most important because they renew our faith in God. Both memorials matter. Both give glory to God.

(Matthew 6:4, Colossians 3:23–24)

PORTRAITS IN THE STONES

The stones carried out of Jordan and the stones left in the river paint a portrait of the gospel itself. Twelve stones buried beneath the waters picture death and burial. Twelve stones lifted out and set on the bank picture resurrection and new life. Together, they proclaim the story of salvation. Romans 6:4 says, “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.” Just as Israel left behind the stones in Jordan, so we leave behind the old life when we are raised with Christ. The stones on the bank declare that new life has begun. These memorials also point forward to the kingdom of God. Joshua crossed over the Jordan River and opened the Land of Promise to all Israel. He set up 12 stones to transmit the message of these actions for all generations. One day Jesus Christ, greater Joshua, crossed over the Jordan River, death, and opened the New Testament Land of Promise, the Kingdom of Heaven. (Matthew 16) The Kingdom of Heaven was opened to all Israel, anyone who believes in Jesus Christ and becomes a child of God. He set up 12 stones, 12 apostles, to transmit the message, the Good News of the Gospel, for all generations.

One day, all nations will know the Lord’s power and bow before Him. Joshua said the stones were set up “that all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty: that ye might fear the LORD your God for ever” (Joshua 4:24). The God who delivered Israel across the river will one day reign in righteousness over all the earth. (Revelation 21:3–4, Philippians 2:9–11)

REMEMBER AND REHEARSE

The Jordan memorials call us to remember what God has done and rehearse it often. Forgetting is the first step toward drifting. But remembering keeps faith alive and strengthens the next generation. Every believer needs both kinds of stones—public testimonies and private devotion. When the children ask, “What mean these stones?” we should be ready with stories of God’s faithfulness. The stones still speak: “The Lord is faithful. The Lord is mighty. The Lord is with His people.” (Lamentations 3:22–23, Hebrews 13:8)
