Chapter 10 — Gilgal

THE FEAR OF THE ENEMY

When the Jordan River rolled back at God’s command and Israel crossed on dry ground, the nations of Canaan knew their days were numbered. These people had heard of Israel, their God, and the great victories they experienced. When Israel came into town, the Canaanites knew their goose was cooked. Listen to Rahab’s account of the Canaanite’s fear of Israel. “For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red sea for you, when ye came out of Egypt; and what ye did unto the two kings of the Amorites, that were on the other side Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom ye utterly destroyed. And as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.” (Joshua 2:10-11 also see Joshua 5:1) No walls of Jericho could stand, no armies could prevail. God Himself had gone before His people.

Fear seized the enemy and faith stirred Israel. Every miracle God works is not only for our encouragement but also for the defeat of our enemies. When the devil sees God’s power active in your life, he trembles. Yet, strangely, God’s people are often more fearful of the enemy than the enemy is of them. Israel would soon learn that the Lord was fighting for them.

(Exodus 15:14-16, Deuteronomy 2:25, James 2:19)

THE REPROACH ROLLED AWAY

At Gilgal, God told Joshua, “This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you. Wherefore the name of the place is called Gilgal unto this day” (Joshua 5:9). Gilgal means “rolling.” For forty years Israel had carried the shame of disobedience, wandering in circles while an entire generation perished. But at Gilgal, God drew a line in the sand. The past was over; the reproach was rolled away.

This is what God does for His people. He not only delivers us from Egypt, but He also removes the shame of Egypt from us. Sin carries reproach—guilt, bondage, accusation. But when God brings us into His promise, He rolls it away. The cross of Christ is our Gilgal, where the burden of sin falls off and the child of God rises to walk in newness of life.

(Romans 8:1, Colossians 2:13-15, Psalm 32:1-2)

A COVENANT RENEWED

Before Israel could march around Jericho, they had to renew the covenant. God commanded that the men be circumcised—a painful act, especially on the edge of battle. Yet obedience comes before victory. Circumcision was a sign that they belonged to God, set apart for His purposes. (Genesis 17:10-11, Deuteronomy 30:6) In the New Testament, circumcision points to something greater. Paul said, “In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands… by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11). In Christ, the old man is cut away, and the believer is made new. Baptism pictures this same reality—dying to self and rising to walk in the newness of life in Christ. Baptism is New Testament circumcision. Israel could not conquer Canaan in the flesh, and neither can we. The battles ahead require hearts surrendered and obedient to God’s purposes. (Romans 6:3-4, Galatians 5:24)

A FEAST REMEMBERED

Once the covenant was renewed, Israel kept the Passover. “And the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the month at even in the plains of Jericho” (Joshua 5:10). Forty years earlier, a lamb’s blood on the doorposts had spared them from judgment in Egypt. Now, in the Promised Land, they remembered again: redemption comes only through the blood.

The Passover looked forward to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Every detail pointed to Christ: the lamb without blemish, the blood applied, the meal shared in faith. As Israel remembered, so must we. We too have a feast of remembrance—Communion, the Lord’s Supper. When we gather around the Lord’s Table, we proclaim His death, remember His sacrifice, and renew our faith in the One who delivers us from judgment.

(Exodus 12:3-14, 1 Corinthians 5:7; 11:23-34, Luke 22:19-20)

A NEW PROVISION

“And they did eat of the old corn of the land on the morrow after the passover… and the manna ceased on the morrow after they had eaten of the old corn of the land” (Joshua 5:11-12). For forty years, God had fed His people daily with manna. But now, the wilderness was behind them, and the land of promise before them. The diet of pilgrims gave way to the harvest of inheritance. The day Israel ate of the corn of the land, the manna ceased.

God’s provision changes as His purposes advance. What sustained you in one season may not carry you in the next. The manna was a miracle, but it was never meant to be permanent. The land flowing with milk and honey was always the goal. In the Christian life, God calls us to grow from milk to meat, from daily survival to fruitful abundance. He gives new strength for new seasons. (Deuteronomy 8:7-10, Hebrews 5:12-14, Philippians 4:19)

THE LESSON OF GILGAL

Gilgal was Israel’s base camp for conquest. It was the place of rolled-away reproach, renewed covenants, remembered redemption, and fresh provision. Every believer needs a Gilgal—a place to circle back, remember what God has done, and renew commitment for what lies ahead. At Gilgal, God turned wanderers into warriors. He still does the same today.

Chapter 11 — An Encounter with God

Ordinary Ground, Holy Ground Joshua stood near Jericho, staring at the fortified city that loomed before Israel. His mind was no doubt heavy with the weight of responsibility. Then it happened. Scripture says, “And it came to pass, when Joshua was by Jericho, that he lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand.” (Joshua 5:13) Joshua was likely burdened with the cares of leading God’s people. Why else would an experienced military commander have his eyes down in enemy territory? I picture Joshua, pacing back and forth, praying for the direction of his next move. Now, an apparent enemy caught him off guard. This was no vision. It was no dream. A man with a sword stood in his path. Joshua asked the natural question: “Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” But the reply startled him: “Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come.” (Joshua 5:14) Joshua realized he was in the presence of God Himself and fell on his face in worship. Notice where this encounter took place. Not in the temple. Not in the tabernacle. Not on a mountain. It was outside Jericho, in an everyday place, when God showed up. Moses had his burning bush while tending sheep on the backside of the desert (Exodus 3:1-4). David was just a shepherd boy when God set His eyes on him (1 Samuel 16:11-13). God delights to meet His people in ordinary places, doing ordinary tasks, and then calls them into extraordinary work. (1 Corinthians 1:26-29)

SLOW RECOGNITION

Joshua didn’t immediately recognize who stood before him. At first glance, he thought this was just another soldier, maybe an ally or an enemy. Only after hearing His words did Joshua realize he was speaking with the Captain of the Lord’s host. Moses too did not understand at first. When he saw the bush that burned, he said, “I will now turn aside, and see this great sight.” (Exodus 3:3) Only then did God call to him out of the bush, “Moses, Moses.” (Exodus 3:4) God often comes to us in ways we do not at first perceive. Young Samuel heard the voice of God three times before realizing it was the Lord (1 Samuel 3:1-10). So it is with us. God may be speaking to us by His Spirit through His Word, prayer, circumstances, or His church, yet we do not immediately recognize Him. But He is patient. He calls until we understand. (1 Samuel 3, Jonah 3)

A HOLY ASSIGNMENT

Encounters with God always come before a calling. Moses’ burning bush moment was followed by the charge to confront Pharaoh: “Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people.” (Exodus 3:10) Joshua’s encounter was followed by God’s declaration: “See, I have given into thine hand Jericho, and the king thereof, and the mighty men of valour.” (Joshua 6:2) There are no “small assignments” in God’s kingdom. Every calling — whether leading a nation, raising children, serving in a local church, or sharing the gospel with a neighbor — is weighty because it comes from the King of Heaven. God meets us, prepares us, and then sends us forward with His power.

(Ephesians 2:10, Philippians 2:13)

WORSHIP ON HOLY GROUND

When Joshua realized who stood before him, he fell on his face and worshiped. “And Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship, and said unto him, What saith my lord unto his servant?” (Joshua 5:14) Immediately the Captain said, “Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy.” (Joshua 5:15) This was the same instruction Moses heard at the burning bush: “Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5) The removal of sandals was more than custom — it symbolized reverence. Sandals are manmade. They are designed to protect from rough ground. But before the presence of the Lord, no manmade barrier may remain. God Himself would guide and protect Joshua’s steps. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.” (Proverbs 9:10) True worship acknowledges that He is holy, and we are His servants. Joshua asked, “What saith my lord unto his servant?” When you encounter God, the right response is not a list of requests but a heart bowed in surrender.

TOTAL SURRENDER

Joshua, the leader of Israel, bowed as a servant before his Captain. Though entrusted with authority, he recognized the Ultimate Authority above him. “Though Joshua was Israel’s leader, he was still subordinate to God; the Ultimate Leader.” Every genuine encounter with God calls for surrender. Moses left Midian to face Pharaoh. Saul of Tarsus, trembling on the Damascus road, asked, “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” (Acts 9:6) Even Christ, in His humanity, prayed in submission to the Father, “Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42) Surrender is not weakness — it is strength yielded to God’s hand. It is trusting His wisdom over our own. It is moving forward in His power rather than our limitations. When Joshua bowed, he found strength to rise and lead.

VICTORY THROUGH GOD’S PRESENCE

This encounter prepared Joshua for Jericho. Days later, the walls fell flat as Israel marched in obedience and faith (Joshua 6:20). Victory was not Joshua’s achievement — it was God’s. Moses’ burning bush led to Israel’s deliverance from Egyptian tyranny; Joshua’s encounter with the Captain of the Lord’s host led to Jericho’s collapse. In both cases, God Himself fought for His people. (Exodus 14:13-14, Zechariah 4:6) Every victory in the Christian life begins the same way: with God’s presence. It is not our strategies, not our wisdom, not our might. It is the Lord who wins the battle. “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.” (Proverbs 21:31)

Chapter 12 — Jericho Falls

THE WALLS OF JERICHO

For twenty-eight long years, the Berlin Wall loomed like a scar across the heart of Europe. Gray, unyielding, and topped with barbed wire, it was more than concrete. It was the symbol of division: East against West, communism against capitalism, oppression against freedom. Families were split, friends torn apart, and dreams crushed under the watchful eyes of armed guards. The removal of this wall seemed as impossible as an end to the Cold War. Yet, one astonishing night, the impossible happened.

The Wall had been built to last, but the dream of freedom never died. Whispers of hope carried through border towns and were kept alive by those who dared to dream. In 1987, U.S. President Ronald Reagan stood before the Brandenburg Gate and bravely cried his famous challenge, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!” To some, these were nothing more than empty political jargon, but to others, those words were a spark. The wall may have been concrete and steel, but the will to break it was human.

Then came that improbable night - November 9, 1989. A German spokesman, Gunter Schabowski, announced that new travel laws would take effect immediately. The news spread like wildfire. Thousands rushed to checkpoints, hearts pounding. Would the guards shoot? Were they free to cross? Was this a trick?

Bewildered guards did the unthinkable - they opened the gates! In an instant, the impossible became a reality. Germans surged across, through, and even over, the Wall that once imprisoned them. Sledgehammers rang like church bells of freedom. Concrete that stood for decades crumbled in hours. President Reagan’s words, “Tear down this wall” had become flesh and blood, hammer and chisel, laughter and tears. The fall of the Berlin Wall was improbable, but not impossible - its end proved, once again, that no man-made barrier is eternal. Even the most immovable walls can crumble.

Like the Berlin Wall for Germans, Jericho stood as a problem for Israel - a city with walls so high and strong it looked impossible to conquer. Jericho was a fortress, locked up tight because of Israel. No one went out, and no one came in. (Joshua 6:1) From a human standpoint, this was an obstacle too big to overcome. Yet God had already declared the outcome: “See, I have given into thine hand Jericho, and the king thereof, and the mighty men of valour.” (Joshua 6:2) Before a single trumpet blew or a single step was taken, God spoke in past tense—“I have given.” The victory was settled before the battle began. The only question was whether Israel would trust His word enough to obey His way.

(2 Corinthians 5:7, Hebrews 11:30)

UNUSUAL TACTICS

God’s plan didn’t look like a military strategy. It looked more like a parade. March around the city once a day for six days. On the seventh day, march seven times, blow the trumpets, and shout. Then the walls will fall. (Joshua 6:3-5) No battering rams. No siege towers. No ladders. Just steps, silence, and a shout. Why would God give such strange instructions? Because He wanted Israel to know the victory was His, not theirs. If the walls had fallen to Israel’s strength, they might have thought, Look what we accomplished. But when they fell to God’s word, there was no mistaking who deserved the glory. (1 Corinthians 1:27-29, Zechariah 4:6) God’s ways often seem unusual, but they are always unstoppable. To paraphrase E.M. Bounds, the world is looking for better methods, but God is looking for better men who understand the power of the Holy Spirit, wise strategy, and steadfast courage.

UNASKED QUESTIONS

Think of all the questions Israel could have asked: Why march? Why seven days? Why so much silence? Yet the people obeyed without debate. Scripture says, “So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests… and they went.” (Joshua 6:6-8) There was no recorded argument, no Kadesh-barnea murmuring, no wilderness rebellion. They simply followed. Faith doesn’t need every answer. It doesn’t demand God explain Himself first. Faith walks even when the plan doesn’t make sense. The Israelites may not have understood why the method mattered, but they trusted the God who gave it.

(Hebrews 11:1, Proverbs 3:5-6)

UNSEEN RESULTS

For six days, nothing happened. No cracks in the walls. No shifting stones. No visible progress. From the outside, obedience may have looked pointless. But unseen results were building. Each day of silent marching was a step of trust that prepared them for the shout of victory. Obedience is often like that. You pray, but don’t see the answer yet. You witness, but don’t see the fruit. You serve, but don’t see the impact. Yet God is at work behind the scenes. The seventh day always comes. The walls always fall when God says the time is right. (Galatians 6:9, Isaiah 55:11) Faith isn’t proven by instant results, but by steady obedience when nothing seems to change.

UNTOUCHABLE SPOILS

When the walls fell, Israel was told not to touch the spoil of Jericho. “And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing… but all the silver, and gold, and vessels of brass and iron, are consecrated unto the LORD.” (Joshua 6:18-19) This first city belonged wholly to God. The temptation would be strong to grab what looked valuable—but obedience demanded surrender. God was teaching them a principle: the first belongs to Him. Jericho was the tithe of Canaan, set apart as holy. The spoils were untouchable because God had claimed them. Whenever we hold back what belongs to the Lord, we forfeit blessing. But when we give Him first place, He pours out more than we could ever claim for ourselves. (Proverbs 3:9-10, Malachi 3:10)

UNBUILDABLE CITY

After Jericho fell, God placed a curse on anyone who would rebuild it: “Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho.” (Joshua 6:26) Centuries later, in the days of Ahab, a man named Hiel tried—and he paid for it with the lives of his sons. (1 Kings 16:34) What God tears down must stay down. When a couple is married, the minister often recites the Scripture from Matthew 19:6, “... What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” The opposite also stands true - What God hath put asunder, let no man join together. We could call this the Jericho principle. This is a warning for us: don’t try to rebuild what God has already destroyed in your life. If He’s given victory over sin, don’t go back and lay its foundation again. What Jericho is God calling you to leave buried? (Romans 6:11-13, Galatians 5:1) Never rebuild the walls God has already brought down.

THE FALL AND THE FAITH

Jericho’s walls fell flat, but not because of Israel’s might. “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days.” (Hebrews 11:30) Faith heard God’s word, walked God’s way, and waited for God’s timing. The lesson of Jericho is clear: God brings victory when His people walk by faith, obey without question, and give Him the glory.

Chapter 13 — Trespass to Triumph

TRESPASS IN THE CAMP

The story of Achan is one of the darkest in Israel’s history. After the mighty walls of Jericho fell, the people should have been overflowing with gratitude and victory. Yet, Scripture begins Joshua 7 with a chilling line: “But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing.” God had given clear instruction: all the spoils of Jericho belonged to Him alone, placed under the ban as devoted to the Lord (Joshua 6:17–19). God said it plainly—Israel had trespassed. One man’s secret sin was counted as the nation’s guilt. Achan had taken a Babylonian garment, silver, and gold, hiding them in the floor of his tent. He may have thought no one would notice, but God always notices. When God’s people treat His commands as mere suggestions, the whole camp suffers. (Ecclesiastes 12:14; Numbers 32:23) Sin is never isolated to an individual; it spreads, it weakens, and it brings defeat.

❝ Strong men go to god in moments of weakness ❞

NEGLIGENT SCOUTING

After Jericho’s victory, Israel set its sights on the smaller city of Ai. The spies returned with confidence: “Let not all the people go up; but let about two or three thousand men go up and smite Ai” (Joshua 7:3). They believed Ai was an easy win. But they left God out of the equation. They presumed success without prayer, without searching their hearts, and without seeking God’s direction. What followed was disaster: thirty-six men were killed, and Israel’s army fled before their enemies (Joshua 7:5). It was the first defeat in the land of victory. Pride often follows victory. We think the next challenge will be easier, the next step will take less prayer, the next battle will require less dependence on God. But neglecting God in the “little” battles leads to devastating failure. (Proverbs 16:18; John 15:5)

FEAR GRIPS ISRAEL

As news of the defeat spread, “the hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Joshua 7:5). Fear paralyzed the nation. The same people who had watched Jericho’s walls crumble now trembled before a small hill town. Fear always magnifies the enemy and minimizes God. Fear encounters one setback, one unanswered prayer, one defeat, and assumes all hope is lost. Israel failed to realize the problem wasn’t Ai’s strength—it was their sin. Until the trespass in the camp was dealt with, every step forward would end in failure. (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 41:10)

JOSHUA’S PRAYER

Broken and confused, Joshua fell on his face before the Lord. “Alas, O Lord GOD, wherefore hast thou at all brought this people over Jordan, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us?” (Joshua 7:7). He tore his clothes and lay before the ark of the Lord until evening. Joshua was a strong man, but even strong men collapse under the weight of defeat. In his broken bewilderment, Joshua turned to God. Where a man turns in defeat says a great deal about his heart and character. Strong men go to God in moments of weakness.

Joshua poured out his confusion, his despair, and even his questions before God. He could not understand why victory had turned to defeat. Yet even in his brokenness, he was in the right place—on his face before the Lord. Prayer is not only for moments of triumph; it is a lifeline for the weary and the wounded.

(Psalm 34:17–18; Philippians 4:6–7)

GOD’S ANSWER

God’s reply was clear and crisp: “Get thee up; wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face? Israel hath sinned” (Joshua 7:10–11). The problem wasn’t with God’s power—it was with Israel’s disobedience. There could be no victory until the sin was exposed and removed. The hidden treasure buried in Achan’s tent had brought an entire nation to its knees. God demanded holiness in the camp before His blessing could return. (Isaiah 59:2; 1 John 1:9) The following day, Achan confessed, his family and possessions were destroyed, and Israel buried them. Israel had reached rock bottom, but from there God could rebuild. Rock bottom is a difficult place to be, but a great place to build. The valley of defeat became the bedrock of victory.

LESSONS FROM THE VALLEY OF DEFEAT

Defeat doesn’t mean God has abandoned us; often, it means there’s something God wants to uncover in us. Israel’s failure at Ai revealed pride, prayerlessness, and hidden sin. And God, in His mercy, used the pain of defeat to bring His people back to Himself. When life collapses, the question is not, “Why did God fail me?” but, “What is God showing me?” The valley is not the end—it is often the place where God begins His deepest work. (Hebrews 12:5–11; James 4:6–10)

ENCOURAGEMENT AFTER DEFEAT

Israel stood shaken. The sting of failure at Ai burned fresh in their minds, and the tragic death of Achan left them sobered. Yet God, like a loving Father, came near with words of encouragement: “Fear not, neither be thou dismayed: take all the people of war with thee, and arise, go up to Ai: see, I have given into thy hand the king of Ai, and his people, and his city, and his land” (Joshua 8:1). When they staggered, He reminded them of His promise. Like a father picking up a child who has fallen from a bicycle, God steadied His people, brushed off their dust, bandaged their scraped knee, and prepared them to ride again. (Psalm 30:5; Micah 7:8; Hebrews 12:11)

HUMBLING BATTLE TACTICS

The next instructions were surprising. Ai was a small city of twelve thousand, yet God commanded Joshua to send all Israel’s six hundred thousand warriors into the campaign. From a human standpoint, it seemed unnecessary—like using a sledgehammer to swat a fly. But God’s ways are higher than ours. What looked foolish to men was wisdom from above. (Isaiah 55:8-9; 1 Corinthians 1:25) Not only was the size of the force humbling, but the strategy itself required Israel to appear weak. Joshua and his men would feign defeat, retreating into the wilderness so Ai’s soldiers would pursue. Only then would those that lay in ambush spring into action. Israel had to look beaten in order to be victorious. Sometimes, following God’s plan means being misunderstood or appearing foolish in the world’s eyes. But faith trusts that God’s ways always lead to true victory. (2 Corinthians 12:9-10; Philippians 2:5-8) Are you willing to appear foolish or defeated in the eyes of men to conquer for the Kingdom of God?

TOTAL VICTORY

God’s plan unfolded flawlessly. “There was not a man left in Ai or Bethel, that went not out after Israel: and they left the city open, and pursued after Israel” (Joshua 8:17). At that very moment, Joshua stretched out his spear toward the city, just as Moses had once lifted his rod over the Red Sea. As long as his hand was raised, Israel prevailed. The enemies who mocked Israel’s retreat suddenly realized too late that God Himself was fighting. (Exodus 17:11; Romans 8:31) By sunset, Ai was in ruins, its king executed, and a great heap of stones raised as a reminder of God’s justice and victory. What began as humiliation ended in triumph—not because of Israel’s strength, but because of God’s faithfulness. Our enemies, too, quickly learn to fear the weapons God places in His people’s hands when those weapons are lifted in obedience and faith. (2 Corinthians 10:4; Psalm 44:3)

AN ALTAR IS BUILT

After the battle, Joshua led the people to Mount Ebal to build an altar unto the Lord. This was no ordinary monument—it was obedience to God’s command through Moses. The altar was made of whole stones, untouched by human tools, a picture of worship uncorrupted by human pride. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were placed upon it, reminding Israel that true victory always leads to true worship. (Deuteronomy 27:1–7; Joshua 8:30–31) In that sacred moment, Joshua wrote a copy of the law upon the stones and read it aloud before the whole congregation.

From the oldest priests and most seasoned warriors, to the youngest children, every ear heard again the blessings and cursings of the covenant. It was a national renewal—a reminder that victory does not rest on military skill but on obedience to God’s Word. This giant worship service, held in a natural amphitheater between two mountains, was the culmination of the promise given to Abraham centuries before. (Genesis 12:6-8) Worship and the Word stood at the center of Israel’s success. (Psalm 19:7-11; Colossians 3:16)

Chapter 14 — Old Wine & Moldy Bread

ISRAEL’S FAME SPREADS

News of Israel’s arrival was spreading like wildfire. Word of Jericho’s walls crumbling and Ai’s defeat echoed across the land. Scripture says, “And it came to pass, when all the kings…heard thereof; that they gathered themselves together, to fight with Joshua and with Israel, with one accord” (Joshua 9:1–2). Fear had gripped the nations. They could see what God was doing. They knew it was only a matter of time before Israel engaged them in battle; they knew God would triumph. They believed their only hope was to fight against God or find a way to survive under His hand.

This sets the stage for Gibeon. Unlike the other kings who chose war, Gibeon chose deceit. They looked at Israel’s God-given momentum and knew they could not win. Instead of humbling themselves and repenting before the Lord, they plotted a lie.

(Psalm 2:1–4, Deuteronomy 7:1–6)

GIBEON’S PLAN

The Bible says, “They did work wilily” (Joshua 9:4). They dressed in worn-out clothes, carried moldy bread, and presented themselves as weary travelers from a far land. It was an elaborate performance, designed to appeal to sight rather than truth. What a picture this is of the enemy of our souls. Satan rarely attacks head-on when he knows he cannot overpower God’s people. Instead, he disguises himself, working through subtlety and craftiness. Like the Gibeonites, he whispers, “We’ ve come from afar. We mean no harm.” But deception is still destruction in disguise. (2 Corinthians 11:14, John 8:44)

OLD WINE AND MOLDY BREAD

Joshua and the princes of Israel fell for it. They looked at the evidence—the worn sandals, the dried bread, the cracked wineskins—and they believed the story. Scripture records the tragedy in a single sentence: “And the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD” (Joshua 9:14).

Imagine it! They were living in the land of milk and honey, yet they sat down to eat moldy bread. How often do we feast on the lies of defeat while standing in the very victory God has given us? How frequently do God’s people trade holiness, power, and the love of God for crude humor, hours of idleness, self-indulgence, and self-centered relationships? How many believers think they are doing “God’s will” while performing self-initiated works of righteousness? Too many believers are eating old wine and moldy bread while living in the land of milk and honey! When we lean on our own understanding, we will misjudge, because human eyes can be fooled but God cannot.

(Proverbs 3:5–6, Isaiah 30:1–2, Psalm 106:13–15)

A COVENANT WITH THE ENEMY

Joshua made peace with them, and the leaders swore an oath before God to let them live (Joshua 9:15). Though the deception was soon uncovered, the covenant stood. Israel could not break their oath without breaking a covenant before God Himself. This decision carried weight for generations. Later, in the days of David, famine came because Saul had violated that covenant by slaughtering the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1–2). What seemed like a small compromise in Joshua’s day carried consequences long after. Sin and compromise always do. A hasty decision without seeking God’s counsel may seem insignificant in the moment, but its impact can echo into the future. (Ecclesiastes 5:4–6, Galatians 6:7–8) Curse or Blessing?

When Israel discovered the truth, they were angry with Gibeon. Israel upheld the covenant of protection, but swore Gibeon would be servants forever. Though cursed to be servants, the Gibeonites were spared and placed in the house of God as “hewers of wood and drawers of water” (Joshua 9:23). What began as deception turned into unexpected mercy. These idolaters, who should have been destroyed, now lived in service near the tabernacle. Later, they became known as the Nethinims, servants of the temple, counted among God’s people in Ezra and Nehemiah’s day. They were a living testimony of Psalm 84:10, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.”

What a reminder and portrait of God’s great grace! We were once outsiders, deceived and deceiving, but God in His mercy has brought us near through Christ. Better to be a doorkeeper in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.

(Psalm 84:10, Ephesians 2:12–13, John 1:12)

APPLICATION FOR US

The tragedy of Joshua 9 is not just that Israel was deceived, but that they forgot to seek the Lord. They relied on sight, on reason, on outward appearances, and it led them into compromise. The warning is clear: whenever we stop seeking God and start leaning on our own wisdom, we are only a step away from making peace with the enemy. But the story also carries hope. Even in failure, God pours out His mercy. The Gibeonites, once liars and outsiders, found a place in the house of God. And Israel, though compromised, would still move forward by God’s grace.

Chapter 15 — The Lost Day

THE BATTLE WITH FIVE KINGS

Israel should not have been in this position. The Gibeonites had deceived them, and instead of seeking the Lord, Joshua and the elders relied on their own wisdom. They made a covenant without seeking God, and that decision set in motion a chain of battles they had not expected. It did not take long for word to spread that Gibeon had made a truce with enemy Israel. This did not sit well with the other pagan kings. Now five Amorite kings had gathered their armies against Gibeon, and Joshua was obligated to fight on their behalf. What Israel’s enemy meant for destruction, God turned into an opportunity. He would once again display His glory through Israel’s missteps. Joshua marched all night from Gilgal, surprising the Amorites at dawn. The Lord Himself fought for Israel, sending panic into the enemy’s camp. Then, as the battle raged, hailstones rained from the heavens, killing more men than Israeli swords. (Joshua 10:8–11, Deuteronomy 9:3, Psalm 18:12–14) God is never trapped by our mistakes. He can take our failures and turn them into a display of His power and mercy.

A PRAYER THAT CHANGED THE HEAVENS

The day of battle stretched on, and Joshua faced a crisis. If the sun went down, the Amorites would escape into the night, regroup, and fight again another day. Victory required more daylight than nature allowed. And so Joshua prayed one of the boldest prayers in all of Scripture: “Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon” (Joshua 10:12). This was not

a casual request. Joshua dared to ask God to alter the very order of creation for the sake of His people. And God answered. “So the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies” (Joshua 10:13). There has never been a day like it. THE SCIENTISTS’ PUZZLE

In Greenbelt, Maryland, a group of space scientists were running complicated computer programs to chart the orbits of the sun, moon, and planets. These calculations were critical—after all, if you’re sending a ship into space, you need to know where the heavenly bodies will be thousands of years in the past or future. But something strange happened. As the computers whirred and printed out their data, the scientists discovered that the numbers didn’t line up. Somewhere, somehow…they were missing a day. Puzzled, they double-checked their equations. They reran the program. They checked every calculation they knew—and still, the results came up short. Time itself was off.

Finally, one of the men on the team hesitated and said, “You know…I remember something from Sunday School. There’s a story in the Bible about the sun standing still.” At first, the others laughed him off. This was science, not Sunday School! But when every scientific solution failed, they reluctantly opened the Scriptures. There it was in Joshua chapter 10: the account of Joshua praying, and the sun standing still so the Israelites could win the battle. The scientists plugged the numbers in. Sure enough, they discovered a missing period of almost a full day—23 hours and 20 minutes. But there was still a problem: forty minutes were unaccounted for. And over thousands of years of orbital patterns, that small gap was enormous.

So they kept searching. They turned to the book of 2 Kings, where God gave King Hezekiah a sign: the shadow of the sundial went backward ten degrees. When they calculated that shift of time, it added up to the missing 120 forty minutes. (2 Kings 20) Together, Joshua’s long day and Hezekiah’s sign explained the mystery. The computer models matched perfectly.

What began as a perplexing problem in astronomy ended with an astounding confirmation of the Scriptures: that the God who made the heavens is also the One who governs time itself. God really did it. The Creator who spoke the world into existence is not bound by the systems He designed. He holds the sun, moon, and stars in His hand. If He says, “Stand still,” they obey. (Colossians 1:16–17, Psalm 19:1–6) The lost day is not just a puzzle for scientists—it is a reminder for believers. Nothing in all creation can stand in the way of God’s promises to His people.

When we pray in line with God’s will, we step into the realm where impossible things happen. God still calls His people to pray prayers that shake heaven and move earth.

(1 John 5:14–15, Ephesians 3:20, Matthew 17:20)

Left to ourselves, we would surely fail. But the God who commands the sun and moon still commands victory for His children.

(Romans 8:31, Exodus 14:14, 2 Chronicles 20:15)

Chapter 16 — Return to Your Tents

ALVIN YORK

Alvin York was a poor farmer from Tennessee who, during World War I, became one of the most decorated American soldiers after leading a daring attack that captured over 130 German soldiers. When he returned home, however, he didn’t pursue fame or politics. Instead, he turned his attention to his family and community. He married Gracie, his childhood sweetheart, and together they raised a large family. Alvin worked tirelessly to provide for them, farming the land and teaching his children faith, humility, and service. Though he was often urged to profit from his “war hero” status, Alvin York refused, saying his duty was to live quietly and set an example at home. Later, he also advocated for better education in rural Tennessee so his children, and others like them, would have opportunities he never had. For Alvin York, his success on the battlefield mattered less than building a strong family rooted in values; values that would endure long after the war.

A RETURN WITH PURPOSE

The land was largely subdued. Battles had been fought, cities conquered, kings defeated, and Israel now stood in a place of rest. For the first time in years, families could breathe without the looming shadow of giants or armies pressing in. It was here, at this point of rest, that Joshua gathered the tribes and gave a surprising command: “Return ye… unto your tents.” (Joshua 22:4) Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Menasseh had kept their promise to fight until the land was subdued. They kept their word. Joshua was not dismissing the people into laziness. He was reminding them that their most important responsibility was at home; to their wives and children. The fight for the land was not the sum total of their God given responsibility. What they did when they returned home would matter as much as what they had done on the battlefield. (Deuteronomy 12:8-10, Hebrews 4:9-11)

FAITHFULNESS IN THE ORDINARY

On the battlefield, obedience looked like courage; sword in hand. But in their tents, obedience would look like devotion, worship, and day-by-day living in the fear of the Lord. Joshua’s charge reminded the people that faith is not only proven in the heat of combat but also in the quiet rhythms of daily life. (Micah 6:8, Colossians 3:17) Sometimes, the harder fight is not out there against the visible enemy but internally—inside the heart, inside the home. When the noise of war fades and routine sets in, we can forget God just as quickly as Israel did in the wilderness. The call to “return to your tents” was not a dismissal from duty but a redirection to continue serving God in the private places where no army watched.

GUARDING THE HEART OF WORSHIP

Joshua’s words came with an emphasis: “Take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law… to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways, and to keep his commandments, and to cleave unto him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.” (Joshua 22:5) The danger was not that Israel would suddenly deny God in public, but that they would drift from Him in private. Sin rarely begins with a shout of rebellion; it usually begins with a whisper of neglect. That is why Joshua urged them to cleave to the Lord—not loosely, not occasionally, but tightly, continually, with a grip that would not let go. (Deuteronomy 10:12-13, John 15:4-5)

Faithfulness at home meant keeping God at the center of their homes. Achan chose to put money, worldly possessions, and disobedience to God’s commands, at the center of his tent. Joshua charged his men to put speaking God’s Word to their children, remembering His covenant at their tables, and letting His commandments guide their steps, first in their homes. Without God and His Word, Israel would again find their hearts wandering.

WHEN ZEAL TURNS INTO DIVISION

Not long after Joshua dismissed the people, a controversy arose. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh built a great altar by the Jordan. Word spread quickly: “They’ve built their own altar! They’re turning from the Lord!” (Joshua 22:10-12) The other tribes gathered for war, ready to purge idolatry from their midst. However, the altar was not for sacrifice but for remembrance. It was meant as a witness that the Lord was God of all the tribes—on both sides of the Jordan. What looked like compromise was, in fact, an act of devotion. Israel nearly went to war with their brothers over a misunderstanding. (Proverbs 18:13, John 7:24, Ephesians 4:3) This moment shows us how easily zeal, even for the right things, can twist into division if we rush to judgment without seeking truth. Unity among God’s people is precious, and it requires carefulness to listen, discern, and remember that the Lord Himself is the center of worship, not our preferences and assumptions.

A WITNESS ACROSS GENERATIONS

The tribes explained their heart clearly: “God forbid that we should rebel against the LORD.” Their altar was not rebellion—it was testimony. They feared that future generations might one day question whether the tribes across the Jordan truly belonged to Israel. So they built a memorial witness, declaring, “The LORD is God.” (Joshua 22:22, 27, 34) This altar, misunderstood at first, became a powerful reminder of identity and unity. It stood to tell their children and their children’s children: We belong to the Lord. We are part of His covenant people. In the same way, our lives are meant to be living witnesses that point future generations to Christ. (Psalm 78:4-7, Matthew 5:16, 2 Timothy 1:5) When God’s people live with this kind of forward-looking faith, they do not just return to their tents for comfort—they return with purpose, building memorials that declare His faithfulness and pass on His truth.

Meditative Thoughts:

• Where is God calling you to be faithful in the “tent”—in the quiet and ordinary places of your life? (Colossians 3:23)

• Have you ever judged a situation before hearing the whole story? How can you better pursue peace and unity among believers? (James 1:19)

• What witness are you leaving for the next generation?

How will your children—or others who follow you—know that “the Lord is God”? (Joshua 24:15)

• Are you cleaving to the Lord today, or loosening your grip through neglect? (Deuteronomy 30:20)

• What “altar of remembrance” can you build in your life to declare His faithfulness? (1 Samuel 7:12)
Chapter 17 — Cities of Refuge

GOD’S PROVISION OF SAFETY

Brandon Lee, the son of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, was an actor and martial artist himself. In 1993, he was filming a movie in Wilmington, North Carolina. During a scene where his character was supposed to be shot, a prop gun was used. Unknown to the cast and crew, the revolver had been improperly prepared. A fragment of a real bullet had accidentally remained lodged in the barrel from an earlier scene. When the blank round was fired, it propelled the fragment out with the force of a live bullet. The round struck Brandon Lee in the abdomen. He was rushed to the hospital, but after hours of surgery, he died at just 28 years old. His death was ruled an accidental homicide—not murder, not suicide, but the tragic result of negligence in handling firearms on set. The incident led to widespread changes in safety protocols regarding prop weapons. Sadly, his passing became one of the most famous accidental deaths in film history.

When Israel entered the land, God did not just give them homes and fields—He gave them safety. Among the cities scattered throughout Canaan, six were chosen by God as cities of refuge. “Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses: That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood” (Joshua 20:2–3). These cities were not man’s idea—they were God’s. He knew the hearts of His people. He knew there would be anger, accidents, misunderstandings, and revenge. He made a way for mercy in the middle of judgment, a place of safety in the midst of fear. Each of these cities pointed forward to Christ, our true Refuge, who welcomes sinners fleeing from the wrath to come.

(Numbers 35:9–15, Hebrews 6:18–20)

THE AVENGER OF BLOOD

The culture of the day demanded blood for blood. If a man was killed, even unintentionally, a near relative was expected to avenge his death. He was called the “avenger of blood.” There was no time for careful trial or measured justice—vengeance was swift and severe. Imagine the fear of the man who swung an axe and watched the head fly from the handle, striking his neighbor. No malice. No intention. But suddenly, the weight of another man’s life was upon him, and the sound of his neighbor’s family crying for vengeance was in his ears. He had only one hope: run to the city of refuge. (Deuteronomy 19:4–6)

RUNNING TO SAFETY

The cities of refuge were placed so that no one in Israel was far from one. The moment his feet crossed the threshold of the refuge city, the avenger could not touch him. This is a picture of salvation. The sinner, condemned already, has only one hope: run to Christ. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10). God has made the way clear. The cross is the signpost. Grace is the open road. There is no barrier between the guilty soul and the Savior except delay. Safety is not found in arguing your case or proving your innocence—it is found in getting to Him. (John 14:6, Romans 8:1)

Abner and Joab:

A MISSED REFUGE

The story of Abner and Joab reminds us of the tragedy of ignoring God’s refuge. Abner, Saul’s general, killed Joab’s brother Asahel in the heat of battle. Later, Joab called Abner aside as though to speak with him peacefully, but there he thrust him through and killed him in the gate of Hebron—a city of refuge (2 Samuel 3:27). Abner was standing at the very place of safety, but he had not stepped inside. One step, and the law would have prevented anyone from touching him. But he delayed, and his life was cut short. How many souls stand just outside the gate of salvation—so close to Christ, so near to refuge—yet never enter in? They know about Christ, but they do not know Him personally as Lord and Saviour. One step of faith, one cry for mercy, and they would be safe forever. Delay is deadly.

(Hebrews 2:3, Acts 26:28)

OPEN TO ALL

The cities of refuge were for everyone. Whether Israelite, stranger, or sojourner, the law of God made room for all to run. “These were the cities appointed for all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them, that whosoever killeth any person at unawares might flee thither” (Joshua 20:9). Christ, our Refuge, is the same. His invitation is not exclusive. His grace is not limited; it is open to all. The ground at the cross is level, and the door to the refuge is open wide. “Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13). No matter the past. No matter the guilt. Refuge is open to all. (John 3:16, Revelation 22:17)

DEATH OF THE PRIEST

There was one limitation in the city of refuge: the guilty man had to stay inside until the death of the current high priest. If found outside the city walls, he would not be sheltered from the avenger of blood. After the priest died, the one seeking refuge was free to go home without fear of vengeance. His liberty was tied to the life of another. This points us straight to Christ, our Great High Priest. But unlike the priests of old, He does not die and leave us vulnerable—He has died once and risen forever. His death secures our freedom. His resurrection guarantees our life. “But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able

also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him” (Hebrews 7:24–25). In Jesus the safety never ends. (Hebrews 9:11–12, John 10:28)

Application: Our Refuge Today The cities of refuge were not given to excuse sin but to show mercy. They pointed to a greater reality—that God Himself is our refuge. When guilt overwhelms, when fear chases hard, when the accuser whispers in your ear, there is only one safe place: in Christ. The warning of Abner stands—don’t stop short. Don’t linger at the gate. Don’t admire the city without entering it. Safety is not in knowing about Christ, but in running to Him and resting in Him. And once inside, we find not just protection from wrath but the peace of forgiveness.

(Colossians 1:20, Psalm 46:1)

• Who around me still stands outside, in danger, needing me to point them to safety? (2 Corinthians 5:20)

• Do I trust fully in my Great High Priest, whose death and resurrection make my salvation secure forever? (Hebrews 10:19–22)
Chapter 18 — Joshua - God’s Leader

Text: Joshua 24:14–22 Joshua stands in the pages of Scripture as Israel’s undisputed, God-appointed leader. His life reminds us that true leadership is not self-made but God-shaped. It was the Lord who saved him from slavery in Egypt, the Lord who raised him up under Moses’ mentoring hand, and the Lord who equipped him to take Israel into the land of promise. Joshua never took credit for the victories; he knew that God was the One who developed him into a strong and faithful leader.

Yet we must acknowledge that, while Joshua’s success was clearly attributed to God, Joshua himself practiced practical leadership principles that still apply today. John Maxwell famously preaches, “Everything rises and falls on leadership.” Joshua led God’s people while following His Leader - he exemplified Maxwell’s principle. He grew in transition, built on the past, taught with patience, used symbols to communicate truth, showed passion, made wise decisions, prioritized worship, and blessed those he led. His story offers us a pattern of spiritual leadership that is both practical and profoundly dependent on God.

GROWING THROUGH TRANSITIONS

Most of us resist change. We like the familiar—the same routines, the same comforts. But Joshua spent most of his life in transition. He went from slave to warrior, from follower to commander, from wilderness wanderer to conqueror in the land. While many around him faltered in these changes, Joshua grew. How? He kept his eyes fixed on the One who never changes. The Lord declares in Malachi 3:6, “For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.” Joshua anchored his faith not in shifting circumstances but in the unshakable God of Israel. When everything else moved, God remained the same. While others wasted their wilderness years, Joshua maximized them. Numbers 27:18 tells us, “And the LORD said unto Moses, Take thee Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the spirit, and lay thine hand upon him.” While Israel merely endured the wilderness, Joshua grew. When transition ended, he was the most prepared man in the nation to lead. Wise leaders today do the same—they use seasons of transition to grow in character, wisdom, and intimacy with God.

BUILDING ON THE PAST

A good leader doesn’t despise the past, nor does he live in it. Joshua struck that balance. He knew Israel’s history mattered. Again and again he reminded the people of what God had done—Abraham’s call, the miracle of Isaac, deliverance from Egypt, the parting of the Red Sea, provision in the wilderness, and victories in the land. (Joshua 24:1–13) He rehearsed these stories not as nostalgia but as motivation: “Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth…” (Joshua 24:14). Joshua didn’t try to overhaul or erase Israel’s history; he built upon it. He taught the people that the same God who worked in the past was still working in the present. Leaders today must do the same. We thank God for those who came before us, but we also embrace the “new thing” He is doing (Isaiah 43:19). The past serves as a reminder of God’s faithfulness, and the present is our opportunity to walk in it.

TEACHING WITH PATIENCE

Joshua wasn’t just a commander; he was a teacher. Good leaders know that instruction is as important as direction. Joshua never assumed the people would automatically remember what God had said. He constantly reminded them: “Remember the word which Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you…” (Joshua 1:13). After the battle at Ai, he personally read the entire Law before the people (Joshua 8:35). Imagine that—a military general taking time to teach Scripture. His leadership was marked not just by strategy but by shepherding hearts. Paul later declared that a bishop must be “apt to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). Joshua modeled that truth long before Paul penned it. Patient teaching is slow work, but it bears lasting fruit. Joshua’s willingness to invest in people ensured they understood why they were fighting, Who they were serving, and how they were to live.

USING SYMBOLS AND STORIES

Joshua knew the power of symbols and stories. A sermon might fade from memory, but a stone of remembrance endures. When Israel crossed the Jordan, Joshua commanded twelve stones to be set up: “That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?” (Joshua 4:6). Time and again he used symbols— the fall of Jericho’s walls, the ambush at Ai, even placing feet on the necks of defeated kings (Joshua 10:24)—to drive truth deep into the people’s hearts.

These symbolic actions were effective in driving home the truths Joshua wished to convey. There is no greater example of symbolic actions than Joshua in the battle against the five hill kings. (Joshua 10) After accepting defeat, these kings fled and hid themselves in a cave. The Israelite soldiers had grown up in total fear of the Canaanites and Amorites. They heard the stories of these “giants”. They heard how their fathers were only grasshoppers compared to them. Joshua wanted to show them these giants up close. He commanded the Israeli soldiers to put their feet on the necks of these defeated kings. This was a power move. It put the Israelite in full control and the king in total submission and humility. Joshua helped to illustrate that even these kings were just ordinary men that could be humbled by God. Throughout the remainder of Joshua’s leadership, there is not one mention of a single soldier fearing the enemy. Joshua wasn’t a polished orator, but he knew that a well-told story and a well-placed symbol could communicate more than words alone. Leaders today should learn from him: don’t just teach truth, embody it; don’t just declare principles, display them.

LEADING WITH PASSION

Joshua’s leadership burned with passion. He wasn’t lukewarm or complacent. When the ten spies gave their evil report, he tore his clothes in grief (Numbers 14:6–7). After the defeat at Ai, he fell on his face before God in brokenness (Joshua 7:6). At 110 years old, he still thundered, “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). His passion was visible in how he lived each day. Before battles, he rose early in the morning to lead God’s people (Joshua 6:12; 8:10). One mark of passionate leaders is how they begin their day. Those who awaken in anticipation of what God might do still have passion. Those who reluctantly begin their day may no longer expect God to do anything. To them, it’s ‘just another day.’ Joshua anticipated what God would do. Passion like this is contagious. When leaders show zeal for God’s work, it inspires courage and faith in those who follow.

DECISIVE IN LEADERSHIP

A leader paralyzed by indecision will lose the confidence of his people. Joshua made decisions carefully but promptly when God spoke (Joshua 1:2, 11). He balanced urgency with discernment, never acting rashly but never stalling either. When sin was in the camp, God told him, “Get thee up” (Joshua 7:10). Joshua rose early the next morning to deal with it. When allies at Gibeon cried for help, he ascended with his army without hesitation (Joshua 10:7). Decisive leadership requires courage and trust in God’s direction. Joshua modeled both.

A WORSHIPFUL LEADER

Amid battles and responsibilities, Joshua never neglected his walk with God. The Lord’s charge to him was clear: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night…” (Joshua 1:8). Joshua lived by that command. Before leading Israel across Jordan, he told the people, “Sanctify yourselves: for to morrow the LORD will do wonders among you” (Joshua 3:5). A military general commanding soldiers to prepare for battle by first preparing their hearts—what a testimony! Joshua shows us that real success flows from time with God. Leadership divorced from worship is hollow; leadership rooted in worship is powerful.

BLESSING THOSE HE LED

Perhaps Joshua’s greatest quality was that he didn’t use his followers; he blessed them. When the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh were released to return home, “Joshua blessed them, and sent them away” (Joshua 22:6). He cared more for their obedience to God than for keeping their military strength. At the close of his life, rather than seek honor for himself, Joshua charged the people once more to follow the Lord and even set up a great stone as a witness against them (Joshua 24:26–27). His last act was not self-congratulation but blessing. Great leaders don’t just build institutions; they build people. Joshua’s concern was for Israel’s faithfulness long after he was gone.

Meditative Thoughts:

• Leadership in God’s kingdom is not about position—it is about faithfulness.

• True leaders grow in transitions, build upon God’s past faithfulness, and point people to His promises.

• Teaching, storytelling, and symbols remind us of truth in ways words alone cannot.

• Passion for God’s work must burn in us no matter our age.

• Decisiveness matters—but so does prayerful discernment.

• Worship is the root of lasting leadership.

• The best leaders are those who bless others, not use them.

Joshua was a great leader because he followed the greatest Leader. His life compels us to ask: Am I leading others closer to Christ by the way I live? Am I instructing them to follow me or am I directing them to follow God?
Conclusion — Choose You This Day

Are you ready to follow your Great Leader in total faith and surrender? Or are you still clinging to fear, self-initiated works of righteousness, or self-indulgent works of the flesh? I challenge you, let go and let God lead. Make obeying God’s voice your knee-jerk reaction, not your reluctant last ditch effort to please Him. If you allow Him, God will lead you to places you never thought possible!

The book of Joshua is more than history—it is a mirror. Every promise claimed, every battle fought, every failure endured, every victory won, reflects the life of faith God has called His people to live. Israel’s story was not written for curiosity but for conviction. Paul said, “Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition…” (1 Corinthians 10:11). From the first victory at Rephidim to the first step across Jordan to the final gathering at Shechem, Joshua’s life reminds us that God is faithful. He keeps His promises, He fights for His people, He goes before them, and He never leaves them. What He required of Israel, He still requires of us: trust Him fully, obey Him completely, and worship Him only.

Yet Israel’s story is also a warning. Compromise always costs. Sin always spreads. Delay always weakens faith. The graves in the wilderness and the ruins of Ai testify that God takes obedience seriously. Half-hearted faith cannot inherit the fullness of His blessing. But Joshua’s life points us forward to One greater. Jesus is the true Joshua, the Captain of Our Salvation, who leads us into a better rest (Hebrews 4:8–9). Where Joshua could only give Israel land, Christ gives eternal life. Where Joshua divided an inheritance, Christ secures for us an incorruptible inheritance reserved in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Where Joshua eventually died, Christ lives forever to intercede for us.

That leaves us with a choice—the same one Joshua set before Israel in his final speech: “Choose you this day whom ye will serve… but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Neutrality is not an option. To follow the Lord is life; to turn away is loss. The book of Joshua calls us to courage. To walk by faith when fear shouts. To trust God’s promises when giants seem bigger. To obey His Word when compromise feels easier. To lift our eyes from the wilderness and fix them on the God who makes a way.

The choice is ours. And the invitation still stands. Step forward. Trust Him. Serve Him. The land of promise is before you.
